sections.heading: Intro
sections.content_markdown: Goal templates each have a physiological definition, calorie strategy, dominant training type, typical duration (if applicable), and progress markers. Users can pick a template OR define a fully custom goal in their own words — for custom goals, the AI maps user intent onto the closest template's underlying logic. Goals can have a deadline (e.g. *"100kg bench by 1 September"*, *"first 20K trail in October"*) or be open-ended (e.g. *"get stronger, no rush"*, *"stay healthy long-term"*).

sections.heading: Mesocycle Sequencing (universal rule)
sections.content_markdown:
Every 12-week macrocycle follows: MEV → MAV → MRV with deload anchors.
Volume pattern per mesocycle: weeks 1–3 progressive build · week 4 consolidation
Micro-deload (-30%) when fatigue accumulates mid-block
Full deload (-40%) at end of macrocycle, before next goal transition

entries.heading: A1 · Get lean
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Sharpen your physique with a mild calorie deficit while keeping your strength.
**Technical signature**: `recomp · mild deficit (-10–15%) · compound + Zone 2 · 4–12 weeks · primary-only or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: A trainer with established muscle mass who wants visible definition for an event, summer, photoshoot, or personal milestone. Not a beginner with 20+ kg to lose; not a competitor in deep stage prep.
**Physiological definition**: Mild caloric deficit sufficient to reduce body fat ~0.5–1% per month while preserving lean mass and performance. Muscle retention under deficit requires high protein intake, a maintained training stimulus that signals muscle preservation, and conditioning that expands metabolic capacity rather than burning out recovery budget.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Deficit −10% to −15% of maintenance
Protein 2.0–2.4 g/kg lean body mass
Carbohydrates front-loaded around training; remainder of energy
Fats ~0.8–1.0 g/kg body weight, omega-3 emphasis
Optional refeed days during phases beyond 6–8 weeks
**Dominant training type**: Compound strength to preserve mass + Zone 2 conditioning for metabolic capacity. Not high-volume hypertrophy (impaired recovery under deficit) and not HIIT-stacking (interferes with strength preservation).
**Typical duration**: 4–12 weeks. Longer risks adaptive thermogenesis and performance loss; shorter rarely produces visible change.
**Frequency recommendation**: 4–5 strength sessions/week + 2 Zone 2 sessions/week. Total weekly volume reduced ~20% versus surplus phases to match recovery capacity.
**Progress markers**:
Body fat −0.5 to −1% per month (DEXA, BIA, calipers, or photo)
Waist circumference −1 to −2 cm per month
Strength maintained on key compounds (RDL, squat, press, row)
Recovery: sleep and HRV stable; drops signal excessive deficit
**Common pitfalls**:
Deficit too steep (−25%+): performance crashes, mood/sleep degrade, muscle loss
Adding HIIT "to burn more": interferes with strength preservation
Underestimating protein: 2.0 g/kg LBM is the floor, not the ceiling
Holding deficit beyond 12 weeks without diet break: plateau and metabolic adaptation
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General health maintenance · Glute development (or other single-area focus, if primary deficit is respected)
**Incompatible goals**: Build muscle / lean bulk · Strength peak · Major weight loss · Race prep — long distance
**Sources**:
Helms, Aragon, Fitschen (2014). Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr.
Israetel, Davis, Case, Hoffmann. The Renaissance Diet 2.0 (Renaissance Periodization, 2020).
McDonald, L. The Ultimate Diet 2.0 and articles on body recomposition ([bodyrecomposition.com](http://bodyrecomposition.com)).
Hall et al. (2016). Energy expenditure and body composition changes after an isocaloric ketogenic diet. Am J Clin Nutr.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Target body composition reached — typically -3 to -5% body fat from start, OR waist circumference -5 to -10 cm, OR user-defined target weight reached. Key compound lifts maintained within 5% of starting load. Photos show visible composition shift.
*Window*: Sustained for 2 weeks at the lower end (rules out water/dietary noise); body fat measurement rolling average over 4 weeks.
*Next step*: Transition to maintenance phase (energy at maintenance, training preserved) for at least 8 weeks before considering next directional goal. Direct return to deficit not recommended.
*Detection*: Passive — bodyweight log (daily/weekly), waist circumference log (weekly), strength logs (per session). Photo import optional.

entries.heading: A2 · Build muscle / lean bulk
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Add lean muscle mass with a moderate calorie surplus over 10–16 weeks.
**Technical signature**: `lean bulk · mild surplus (+5–10%) · hypertrophy dominant · 10–16 weeks · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: A trainer with 6–12+ months of consistent strength training who wants visible muscle gain and accepts small fat gain in exchange. Not a beginner just starting out; not someone whose primary concern is body fat percentage right now.
**Physiological definition**: Caloric surplus and progressive overload provide the energy and mechanical stimulus for hypertrophy. Lean bulks emphasize quality of gains (high protein, controlled surplus, structured progression) over rapid weight increase. Recovery and sleep matter more than in maintenance because total weekly volume is higher.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Surplus +5% to +10% of maintenance (~+200 to +400 kcal)
Protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates high, especially around training sessions
Fats ~0.8–1.0 g/kg body weight
Target rate of weight gain 0.25–0.5% per week (faster = disproportionately more fat)
**Dominant training type**: Hypertrophy (8–15 reps, RPE 7–9, MAV→MRV cycling per Layer 3), compound + isolation balance. Conditioning minimal: 1–2× Zone 2 weekly to preserve aerobic base without taxing recovery budget.
**Typical duration**: 10–16 weeks per block. Then either consolidate at maintenance or transition to a brief mini-cut to manage body fat before the next bulk.
**Frequency recommendation**: 4–5 strength sessions/week. Each muscle group hit 2× weekly minimum.
**Progress markers**:
Body weight +0.25–0.5% per week
Strength progressive on key compounds (~+2.5–5% per 2 weeks early in block, slowing later)
Body fat rising slowly — 1–2% increase across the block is expected and acceptable
Photos every 4 weeks: visible muscle change in mirror
**Common pitfalls**:
Surplus too aggressive (+500+ kcal): excessive fat gain with no extra muscle
Adding heavy conditioning: undermines surplus, interferes with recovery
Junk volume: more sets without progression discipline produces fatigue, not growth
Comparing rates to enhanced or genetically gifted lifters: realistic for an intermediate natural is +1–2 kg lean mass per year, less for advanced
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · Glute development / arm focus / single-area aesthetic · General strength
**Incompatible goals**: Get lean / sustainable fat loss / major weight loss · Strength peak · Race prep — long distance
**Sources**:
Schoenfeld, B. (2010). The mechanisms of muscle hypertrophy and their application to resistance training. J Strength Cond Res.
Schoenfeld, B. et al. (2017). Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass. J Sports Sci.
Israetel, M. et al. Scientific Principles of Hypertrophy Training (Renaissance Periodization, 2021).
Helms, Morgan, Valdez. The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Nutrition (2nd ed., 2019).
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Target weight gain reached at expected rate (+0.25-0.5% body weight/week), key compound lifts progressed by ≥10-15% from block start, visible muscle change in 4-week photos. Body fat increase within acceptable 1-2% range.
*Window*: 10-16 weeks per block (matches typical duration); rate-of-gain check at week 4 and week 8 to catch overshoot.
*Next step*: Consolidate at maintenance for 4-8 weeks, OR transition to mini-cut if body fat trended high, OR continue with new block at adjusted surplus.
*Detection*: Passive — bodyweight trend, strength logs, optional photo import every 4 weeks.

entries.heading: A3 · Body recomposition
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Lose fat and gain muscle at the same time — slow but possible if you've been training consistently.
**Technical signature**: `simultaneous fat loss + muscle gain · maintenance to slight deficit (-5%) · strength + hypertrophy mix · 12–24 weeks · advanced users only`
**Who picks this**: A trainer with 1–2+ years of consistent training who doesn't want phase-based diet changes. Best suited to people who can stay disciplined with high protein and structured training over long periods. Not the right pick for novices (better served by dedicated cut or bulk) or for users with significant fat to lose.
**Physiological definition**: Recomposition occurs when training stimulus is strong enough to drive muscle protein synthesis and net muscle gain while a small energy deficit (or near-maintenance with very high protein) drives fat oxidation. The window for simultaneous gain and loss is narrowest in trained users; novices and detrained users see it most easily as "newbie gains under deficit."
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance to −5% (very mild deficit, near-neutral)
Protein 2.2–2.6 g/kg body weight (highest of body comp goals)
Carbohydrates moderate, well-timed around training
Fats ~0.8–1.0 g/kg body weight
Refeeds rarely needed (deficit is too small to require them)
**Dominant training type**: Strength + hypertrophy mix, compound dominant. Conditioning moderate (2× Zone 2 + occasional tempo). Volume held at MAV — pushing MRV under deficit risks regression.
**Typical duration**: 12–24 weeks. Recomp is slow by nature; under 8 weeks is too short to evaluate.
**Frequency recommendation**: 4–5 sessions/week. Each muscle group 2× weekly.
**Progress markers**:
Body weight stable to slight decrease (this is a feature, not a problem)
Strength maintained or slowly progressing
Body fat slow decline (−0.25 to −0.5% per month)
Waist down + arms/legs measurements stable or up
Photo evidence over 8+ weeks (week-to-week change too small to see)
**Common pitfalls**:
Wrong audience: novice and early intermediates see better results from dedicated cut or bulk phases
Impatience: 8 weeks is too short to evaluate progress
Scale obsession: stable weight with composition shift is the desired outcome
Insufficient protein: under 2.0 g/kg, the recomp signal collapses
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General health maintenance · Single-area aesthetic at low–moderate intensity (glute, arm)
**Incompatible goals**: Get lean · Build muscle / lean bulk · Strength peak · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Barakat, C. et al. (2020). Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Strength Cond J.
Garthe, I. et al. (2011). Effect of two different weight-loss rates on body composition and strength and power-related performance in elite athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab.
Longland, T. et al. (2016). Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss. Am J Clin Nutr.
Helms, Morgan, Valdez. The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Nutrition — recomposition chapter.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Body weight stable to slightly lower (±1 kg from start), body fat -1 to -3%, key compounds maintained or up, waist circumference -2 to -5 cm. Photos at 8 and 16 weeks show composition shift.
*Window*: 12-24 weeks (recomp is slow by nature; under 8 weeks not evaluable); rolling 4-week measurements.
*Next step*: Continue recomp if still progressing, OR transition to dedicated cut/bulk if progress stalls for 6+ weeks, OR shift to maintenance.
*Detection*: Passive — bodyweight, strength, waist log. Prompted at week 16: "Are you seeing the change you wanted in the mirror?" (yes/somewhat/no → routing).

entries.heading: A4 · Sustainable fat loss
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Lose 5–15 kg gradually with habits you can keep, rather than rapid changes that bounce back.
**Technical signature**: `fat loss · moderate deficit (-15–20%) · strength preservation + Zone 2 + capacity · 12–26 weeks · habit-focused`
**Who picks this**: Someone with 5–15 kg to lose who values steady, durable change over rapid transformation. Not necessarily a dedicated lifter yet — capacity may be moderate. Most common audience for the body composition cluster.
**Physiological definition**: Moderate caloric deficit produces ~0.5–0.75% body weight loss per week, paired with resistance training for muscle retention and conditioning to expand metabolic capacity. "Sustainable" means: deficit is achievable on most days without willpower fatigue, training supports long-term adherence, and the rate of loss is slow enough to avoid strong adaptive responses (hunger, mood drop, performance crash).
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Deficit −15% to −20% of maintenance
Protein 2.0–2.4 g/kg lean body mass (or 1.6–2.0 g/kg body weight when LBM is unknown)
Carbohydrates moderate, timed around training
Fats ~0.8–1.0 g/kg body weight
Diet break or refeed every 8–12 weeks of continuous deficit
**Dominant training type**: Strength (compounds, 6–10 reps) for muscle retention + Zone 2 (3× weekly) for metabolic capacity. Avoid HIIT-stacking; recovery is the binding constraint under deficit.
**Typical duration**: 12–26 weeks per block. Plan a diet break around week 12 if continuing past it.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3–4 strength sessions + 2–3 Zone 2 sessions weekly. Start lower if conditioning is unfamiliar; build toward this over 4–6 weeks.
**Progress markers**:
Body weight −0.5 to −0.75% per week (~0.4–0.6 kg/week for an 80 kg person)
Use 4-week rolling average; ignore week-to-week noise
Waist circumference steady decrease
Strength maintained on key compounds
Mood and sleep stable. A drop signals deficit too aggressive
Adherence 80%+ of training and nutrition targets hit weekly
**Common pitfalls**:
Targeting 1+ kg/week: not sustainable, muscle loss accelerates
Eliminating entire food groups: hard to maintain, often rebounds
All-or-nothing weeks: 80% adherence weekly beats 100% for 3 weeks then 0%
Replacing strength with cardio: muscle loss accelerates fat regain post-block
**Compatible secondary goals**: General health maintenance · Mobility & joint health · Cardiovascular health focus · Metabolic health
**Incompatible goals**: Build muscle / lean bulk · Strength peak · Race prep — long distance · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Helms, A., Aragon, A., Fitschen, P. (2014). Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr.
Hall, K. et al. (2012). Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet.
Aragon, A. et al. (2017). International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets and body composition. J Int Soc Sports Nutr.
McDonald, L. A Guide to Flexible Dieting (Lyle McDonald, 2005) — practical adherence framework.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Total weight loss target reached (typically -5 to -15 kg depending on starting point), waist circumference target reached, key compounds maintained, sleep and energy reported stable throughout (no crash signals).
*Window*: Variable — depends on starting body composition. Check sustainability at week 12, week 24, and at goal-reached moment (no rebound risk indicators).
*Next step*: Transition to extended maintenance phase (minimum 12 weeks) before any further fat-loss work. If maintenance holds clean, user may set next directional goal.
*Detection*: Passive — bodyweight trend, waist log, sleep/energy self-report data. Prompted at goal moment: "How does this feel — sustainable or like you're hanging on?"

entries.heading: A5 · Major weight loss
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Lose 15+ kg over a year or more by building habits, capacity, and consistency.
**Technical signature**: `significant fat loss · phased deficit · capacity + habit dominant · 52+ weeks · medical-aware`
⚠ **Recommend baseline check with GP and (if possible) dietitian before starting.** If user has obesity-related conditions (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea, weight-bearing joint pain), professional supervision becomes important alongside the app's guidance. The app supplements care, not replaces it.
**Who picks this**: Someone with 15+ kg to lose, often starting from low training capacity. Goal horizon is a year or longer. Recomp methods don't apply — the mechanism is sustained deficit, and capacity-building matters as much as the deficit itself.
**Physiological definition**: Long-term sustained energy deficit produces fat loss; the challenge is not the mechanism but adherence and metabolic adaptation across many months. Phasing deficit periods with maintenance periods (refeeds, diet breaks) preserves adherence and reduces metabolic adaptation. Building capacity (resistance training + low-impact conditioning) is as important as the deficit itself — without it, regain is near-certain.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Deficit −20% to −25% of maintenance during fat-loss phases (lower at start if capacity is low)
Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg target body weight (not actual, when starting BMI is high)
Carbohydrates and fats balanced per personal tolerance
Refeeds 1–2 weeks at maintenance after every 8–12 weeks of deficit
Track weight by 4-week rolling average; week-to-week is too noisy at this scale
**Dominant training type**: Strength training (compounds, scaled to capacity — initially machines and bodyweight, progressing to free weight) + low-impact conditioning (Zone 2 walking, cycling, swimming). HIIT introduced only after baseline aerobic capacity is established (typically months in).
**Typical duration**: 12+ months realistic for 15+ kg. Phase structure: 12 weeks deficit → 2 weeks maintenance → repeat, until target.
**Frequency recommendation**: Start at 2–3 sessions/week if untrained; progress to 4 over months. Daily walking from week 1 (steps target as primary daily-conditioning anchor).
**Progress markers**:
Body weight −0.5 to −1% per week (e.g. 0.5–1 kg/week for a 100 kg person)
4-week rolling average loses noise, captures trend
Waist circumference down steadily
Resting heart rate dropping (cardiovascular adaptation)
Daily steps rising
Strength rising in absolute terms (muscle being added or preserved)
Sleep, mood, energy stable to improving
**Common pitfalls**:
Targeting 1+ kg/week sustained: muscle loss accelerates, regain almost guaranteed
Skipping resistance training: ~25% of weight lost as muscle, rebound at lower metabolic rate
All-deficit, no maintenance phases: adaptation, plateau, breakdown
Starting with high-intensity modalities: joint injury common at higher BMI, blocks progress entirely
Comparing rate of loss to others: variation in real-world outcomes is enormous
**Compatible secondary goals**: Cardiovascular health focus · Metabolic health · General health maintenance · Mobility & joint health
**Incompatible goals**: Build muscle / lean bulk · Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Body recomposition
**Sources**:
The Look AHEAD Research Group (2013). Cardiovascular effects of intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes. NEJM.
Wing, R. & Phelan, S. (2005). Long-term weight loss maintenance. Am J Clin Nutr — National Weight Control Registry findings.
Hall, K. et al. (2016). Persistent metabolic adaptation 6 years after "The Biggest Loser" competition. Obesity.
Müller, M., Bosy-Westphal, A. (2013). Adaptive thermogenesis with weight loss in humans. Obesity.
Israetel, M. et al. The Renaissance Diet 2.0 (Renaissance Periodization, 2020) — phasing structure for long-haul diets.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Weight loss milestone reached (typically -20 kg or -15% body weight, or user-set target). Mobility markers improved (can complete bodyweight movements that were inaccessible at start). Strength rebuilt to functional baseline. Medical markers (if shared) trending favorable.
*Window*: Extended — 6-18 months for major weight loss. Milestone-based progression rather than single-window.
*Next step*: Long-term maintenance with explicit relapse-prevention structure. Periodic reassessment quarterly. Consider transition to general health maintenance (D1) as primary goal.
*Detection*: Passive — bodyweight trend, training capacity (movements unlocked). Prompted quarterly: "Three months at this weight — does it feel sustainable, or are old patterns returning?"

entries.heading: B1 · General strength
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Get stronger across the main lifts without chasing a specific peak — long-term, sustainable progress.
**Technical signature**: `general strength · maintenance kcal · compound dominant · 5–8 reps · open-ended · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Someone who wants to be measurably stronger over months and years without chasing a specific 1RM deadline. The most common strength goal — "ik wil sterker worden, zonder meet." Suitable for novices through advanced; the protocol scales.
**Physiological definition**: Sustained progressive overload across compound lifts in moderate rep ranges (5–8). Primary adaptations are neural (rate coding, motor unit recruitment, intermuscular coordination) plus moderate hypertrophy. Less neurally taxing than peaking blocks, more sustainable across years.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance to slight surplus (+0% to +5%)
Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates moderate to high, around training
Fats ~0.8–1.0 g/kg body weight
**Dominant training type**: Compound lifts (squat, deadlift, bench, press, row) at 5–8 reps, RPE 7–8. Volume cycled MEV→MAV per Layer 3. Conditioning moderate (1–2× Zone 2 weekly) to support recovery without interfering. Accessory work for weak points and structural balance.
**Typical duration**: Open-ended. Run in 8–12 week blocks separated by short deloads. Yearly progress for an intermediate: ~5–10% on main lifts. Slower for advanced, faster for novices.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3–4 strength sessions/week. Each main lift trained 1–2× weekly. Compound coverage across the week: hinge, squat, push, pull.
**Progress markers**:
Working weight at fixed RPE rising over 4–8 week windows
Rep records (5RM, 8RM) rising
Bar speed at submaximal loads improving (subjective signal)
Strength endurance (rep-out at fixed weight) stable or rising
Recovery between sessions stable; deteriorating signals overreach
**Common pitfalls**:
Chasing 1RM weekly: unnecessary for general strength, accumulates fatigue
Program-hopping: switching every 4 weeks blocks long-term overload
Adding volume to "feel like more is happening": violates MAV→MRV logic
Neglecting deloads: compound progress stalls without periodic reset
Skipping the press and row: vertical pull/push imbalance is the most common silent weak point
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · Build muscle / lean bulk (slight overlap, but compatible) · Glute development / arm focus · General health maintenance
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Sustainable fat loss / Major weight loss · Race prep — long distance
**Sources**:
Rippetoe, M. Starting Strength (3rd ed., Aasgaard, 2011).
Helms, E., Morgan, A., Valdez, A. The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Training (2nd ed., 2019).
Schoenfeld, B. et al. (2017). Strength and hypertrophy adaptations between low- vs. high-load resistance training. J Strength Cond Res.
Israetel, Hoffmann, Smith. Scientific Principles of Strength Training (Renaissance Periodization, 2015).
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Key lift targets reached (e.g., bodyweight bench, 1.5× bodyweight squat, 2× bodyweight deadlift for men; scaled equivalents for women), OR user-defined strength target (e.g., "100 kg squat") achieved. Technique quality maintained at target loads.
*Window*: Single-test confirmation — top set held for 2 sessions across a 2-week window (rules out one-off PR).
*Next step*: Transition to strength endurance (B3), strength peak block (B2), or hypertrophy phase (A2). User chooses direction.
*Detection*: Passive — strength logs (1RM equivalents from top sets, RPE-tagged).

entries.heading: B2 · Strength peak
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Push for a personal record on a specific lift on a specific deadline — powerlifting-style.
**Technical signature**: `peaking · maintenance kcal · low rep heavy load (1–5) · 6–8 weeks · deadline-bound · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: Someone with an established strength base (typically 1+ year of consistent training) targeting a specific 1RM by a specific date. Powerlifting meet, personal milestone, or a "test day" before transitioning to another goal. Not the right pick for novices (still gaining from general progression) or for someone without a base lift to peak.
**Physiological definition**: Peaking blocks reduce volume and increase load (intensification) to express maximum strength in the chosen lifts. Adaptations are primarily neural: rate coding, motor unit synchronization, and movement specificity at near-maximal load. Less hypertrophy stimulus and more central fatigue than general strength work; recovery is the binding constraint.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance (deficit caps maximal force output meaningfully)
Protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates moderate to high — central nervous system fuel
Hydration and sleep are non-negotiable; small drops show up in performance immediately
**Dominant training type**: Heavy compounds at 1–5 reps, RPE 7–9, long rest (3–5 min). Accessory work reduced versus general strength block. Conditioning minimal (1× Zone 2 weekly maximum) to preserve recovery for heavy main work. Deload in final week before test day.
**Typical duration**: 6–8 weeks. Beyond 8 weeks of intensification, central fatigue exceeds adaptation and PRs become harder, not easier.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3–4 sessions/week. Main lift practiced 2–3× weekly at heavy intensities. Variations (pause, paused-no-bounce, board-press, etc.) used to maintain stimulus while managing fatigue.
**Progress markers**:
Working weight at fixed RPE rising weekly until taper
Bar speed at submaximal loads visibly faster
1RM test PR on test day
Recovery between sessions stays stable; deterioration signals taper too late
**Common pitfalls**:
Peaking without a base: novice gains belong in general strength, not peaking
Stacking conditioning: HIIT or volume cardio steals from CNS recovery
Going to RPE 10 weekly: nervous-system burnout before test day
Cutting calories: maximum force is energetically expensive; deficit during a peak is sabotage
Skipping the deload week before test: leaves the PR on the table
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · Single-area aesthetic at very low intensity
**Incompatible goals**: General strength · Build muscle / lean bulk · Sustainable fat loss / Major weight loss · Race prep (any distance) · Body recomposition
**Sources**:
Israetel, M., Hoffmann, J., Smith, C.W. Scientific Principles of Strength Training (Renaissance Periodization, 2015).
Zourdos, M. et al. (2016). Novel resistance training-specific RPE scale measuring repetitions in reserve. J Strength Cond Res.
Helms, E., Cronin, J., Storey, A., Zourdos, M. (2016). Application of the repetitions in reserve-based rating of perceived exertion scale for resistance training. Strength Cond J.
Tuchscherer, M. The Reactive Training Manual (Reactive Training Systems, 2008).
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: New 1RM set on target lift(s) at planned peak week. Technique held under maximal load.
*Window*: Single-test on planned peak day. Counts only with planned peak structure (taper preceded, RPE progression respected).
*Next step*: Mandatory deload (1-2 weeks), then transition to hypertrophy (A2), general strength (B1), or extended recovery block. Do NOT chain peak blocks without intervening base.
*Detection*: Passive — top-set log with PR flag. Prompted post-peak: "Recovery as expected, or harder than usual?" (routes deload depth).

entries.heading: B3 · Strength endurance
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Build the strength to keep going — high-rep work capacity for hybrid races, CrossFit-style demands, manual labor.
**Technical signature**: `strength endurance · maintenance kcal · 12–20 reps · short rest · 8–12 weeks · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Someone training for Hyrox, CrossFit-style competition, manual labor demands, or hybrid races where load is moderate but reps and time-under-tension are extended. Also fits team-sport athletes who need repeat-bout capacity (e.g. football midfielders, MMA fighters between rounds).
**Physiological definition**: High-rep work at moderate load (typically 50–70% 1RM) produces local muscular endurance through metabolic stress and capillary density adaptations alongside maintained strength. Cardiovascular contribution is significant — the heart and aerobic system are taxed alongside the muscle. Different training response from pure strength (1–5 reps) or hypertrophy (8–12 reps).
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates moderate to high — fuel for sustained metabolic load
Hydration and electrolytes especially important given conditioning overlap
**Dominant training type**: Compound lifts at 12–20 reps, RPE 7–8, short rest (60–90 sec). Circuit-style supersets aligned with Layer 1 architecture. Conditioning 2–3× weekly (Zone 2 + interval-tempo work) provides cardiovascular base. Strength endurance benefits from Layer 1's existing flow principle.
**Typical duration**: 8–12 weeks per block. Often run as a transition block before or after a peaking phase, or as preparation for a hybrid event.
**Frequency recommendation**: 4 sessions/week. Each muscle group hit 1–2× with high-rep scheme. Conditioning runs alongside without interference (because intensity is moderate).
**Progress markers**:
Reps achieved at fixed weight rising
Recovery between sets improving (HR returns faster)
Time-to-completion on benchmark workouts dropping
Cardiovascular markers: HR drift in Zone 2 <5%, resting HR steady or down
Subjective work capacity: "third set feels like first set" within a block
**Common pitfalls**:
Treating it as easy hypertrophy: rep ranges look similar but rest periods, total volume, and metabolic profile differ significantly
Underestimating cardiovascular cost: this overlaps with conditioning more than other strength goals
Skipping the strength base: high-rep work without prior strength foundation produces fatigue, not endurance
Letting load drift down to RPE 4–5: stimulus too low to drive adaptation
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · Cardiovascular health focus · Hybrid athlete (Hyrox-style) · Combat sports prep · Team sport season prep
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Schoenfeld, B. et al. (2015). Effects of low- vs. high-load resistance training on muscle strength and hypertrophy. J Strength Cond Res.
Bompa, T.O., Buzzichelli, C. Periodization: Theory and Methodology of Training (6th ed., Human Kinetics, 2018).
Coffey, V., Hawley, J. (2017). Concurrent exercise training: Do opposites distract? J Physiol.
Renaissance Periodization. Scientific Principles of Hypertrophy Training — repetition-range continuum chapter.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Target rep capacity reached on key lifts (e.g., 20 strict pull-ups, 30 push-ups, 100 reps total at moderate load in time block). OR functional task: kettlebell complex, sandbag carry, loaded work at target duration.
*Window*: Single test or 2-week confirmation depending on test type.
*Next step*: Transition to general strength (B1), hybrid (C4), or maintenance. User chooses next emphasis.
*Detection*: Passive — set/rep logs, test-day rep counts. Prompted if test is task-based: "Did you complete the [task] without compromise?"

entries.heading: C1 · Race prep — short distance (5K–10K)
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for a fast 5K or 10K — VO2max, lactate threshold, and race pace.
**Technical signature**: `5K–10K race prep · maintenance kcal · VO2max + threshold + race pace · 8–12 weeks · deadline-bound · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: Runner with established aerobic base (can run 30+ minutes continuously) targeting a 5K or 10K race time. Either a first race or a PR attempt. Not the right pick for someone who can't run continuously yet — they need general health / cardiovascular base first.
**Physiological definition**: 5K and 10K performance is dominated by VO2max (peak oxygen uptake), lactate threshold (the pace at which blood lactate begins accumulating), and running economy. Training prescription distributes work across three intensity zones: easy aerobic (~70% of volume), threshold (lactate steady-state pace), and VO2max (3–5 min interval pace). The 80/20 polarized model — 80% easy, 20% hard, minimal middle — outperforms uniformly moderate training.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance (recovery is the binding constraint)
Protein 1.6–1.8 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates high — 5–7 g/kg on training days
Pre-race carbohydrate loading 24–48 hours prior
Hydration and electrolyte planning essential
**Dominant training type**: Easy running (Zone 2, 70%+ of weekly volume) + 1× threshold session + 1× VO2max session weekly. Strength work 1–2× weekly maintained for injury prevention (lower body + posterior chain). Race-pace work introduced in final 4–6 weeks of block.
**Typical duration**: 8–12 weeks per block. Final 7–14 days = taper. First-time racers benefit from longer base period before the structured block; experienced runners can shorten.
**Frequency recommendation**: 4–6 runs/week + 1–2 strength sessions. Total weekly volume scales with experience: novice 25–35 km, intermediate 35–55 km, advanced 50–80 km.
**Progress markers**:
Threshold pace holds for 20–40 minutes at controlled HR
VO2max interval pace rising over the block
Easy pace HR dropping at fixed pace (aerobic adaptation)
Race pace feels controlled in final 4 weeks
Resting HR steady; rises signal recovery deficit
**Common pitfalls**:
Running easy too hard: most common error — easy must be truly easy (conversational pace)
Skipping easy days: high-intensity-only work blocks aerobic base development
Adding intensity weekly without easy week: 3-week build / 1-week recovery rhythm protects against breakdown
Cutting calories during a block: undermines recovery and adaptation
Long runs longer than necessary for distance: 5K block doesn't need 25 km long runs
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General strength (low-volume) · Cardiovascular health focus · Sustainable fat loss only at very mild deficit and only outside peak training weeks
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Race prep — long distance · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Daniels, J. Daniels' Running Formula (4th ed., Human Kinetics, 2022).
Seiler, S. (2010). What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
Magness, S. The Science of Running (Origin Press, 2014).
Pfitzinger, P., Latter, S. Faster Road Racing: 5K to Half Marathon (Human Kinetics, 2014).
Joyner, M., Coyle, E. (2008). Endurance exercise performance: the physiology of champions. J Physiol.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Race day completed at target time/pace, OR final tune-up session hit target pace at planned RPE. Strength volume held through block.
*Window*: Single-test = race day. Pre-race tune-up at week -2 confirms readiness.
*Next step*: Recovery week (active recovery only), then transition to maintenance running (D1/D2), next race block, or different goal direction.
*Detection*: Passive — pace/time from session log, race result import. Prompted post-race: "Hit the time, missed it, or DNF?" (routes recovery and next-cycle planning). Plus post-session checkbox: "Was this a race-simulation?" (flags practice tune-ups at week -2 as event-grade for readiness confirmation).

entries.heading: C2 · Race prep — long distance (half marathon to ultra)
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for a half marathon, marathon, or ultra — aerobic base, running economy, and fueling strategy.
**Technical signature**: `half/full/ultra race prep · maintenance to slight surplus · aerobic base + threshold + long run · 12–20 weeks · deadline-bound · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: Runner targeting 21.1 km, 42.2 km, or longer. Established aerobic base required (can comfortably run 60+ minutes continuously). Goal horizon is 12+ weeks; longer distances need longer prep.
**Physiological definition**: Long-distance running is dominated by aerobic capacity, running economy (energy cost per km), fatigue resistance, and (for marathon+) substrate utilization (the ability to oxidize fat at race pace, sparing glycogen). Training emphasizes high volume in the easy aerobic zone (75–85% of total), structured threshold work, long runs progressing to race-specific durations, and — for marathon and longer — race-pace fueling practice.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance during base, slight surplus during peak training weeks
Protein 1.6–1.8 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates 5–8 g/kg on training days, higher around long runs
Practice race-day fueling (gels, carb drinks) in long runs from week 6+
Hydration and electrolyte plan rehearsed in race conditions
**Dominant training type**: Easy aerobic running (75–85% of volume) + 1× threshold/tempo session + 1× long run weekly. Strength work 1–2× weekly (lower body + core) for injury prevention and economy. Race-pace blocks within long runs introduced in final 6–8 weeks. Taper 2–3 weeks before race.
**Typical duration**:
Half marathon: 12 weeks
Marathon: 16–18 weeks
50K+ ultra: 18–24 weeks
**Frequency recommendation**: 5–6 runs/week + 1–2 strength sessions. Weekly volume scales with distance and experience:
Half marathon 50–80 km
Marathon 60–110 km
Ultra 80–140+ km
**Progress markers**:
Long run distance progressing safely (10% rule per week)
Easy pace HR dropping at fixed pace
Threshold pace sustaining longer (40+ min)
Marathon pace running feels controlled in final 4 weeks
Resting HR and HRV stable
Race-pace fueling tolerated without GI issues
**Common pitfalls**:
Volume jumping too fast: >10–15% weekly increase is the leading injury cause
Long runs too hard: easy long runs build economy; hard long runs accumulate fatigue
Skipping strength work: injury rates rise sharply without it (Achilles, knee, hip)
Neglecting fueling practice: race-day GI failures derail more marathons than fitness gaps
Compressing taper: 2–3 weeks before marathon, <1 week before half
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General strength (low volume) · Cardiovascular health focus
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Race prep — short distance · Strength endurance · Sustainable fat loss / Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Pfitzinger, P., Douglas, S. Advanced Marathoning (3rd ed., Human Kinetics, 2019).
Daniels, J. Daniels' Running Formula (4th ed., 2022).
Stellingwerff, T. (2012). Case study: nutrition and training periodization in three elite marathon runners. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab.
Hoffman, M., Krishnan, E. (2014). Health and exercise-related medical issues among 1,212 ultramarathon runners. PLoS ONE.
Magness, S. The Science of Running (2014).
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Race completed at target time/pace OR completion-as-success (per user intent at goal setup). Long-run progression hit peak distance without injury. Strength volume maintained or scaled down per plan.
*Window*: Single-test = race day. Peak-week long run at week -3 to -4 confirms readiness.
*Next step*: Extended recovery (2-4 weeks active recovery), then maintenance running, next race block, or different goal direction.
*Detection*: Passive — long-run log, weekly mileage, race result. Prompted post-race: "How did the back half feel — controlled or surviving?" Plus post-session checkbox: "Was this a race-simulation?" (flags practice long-runs at week -3 to -4 as event-grade for peak-readiness confirmation).

entries.heading: C3 · Trail running / mountain racing
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for trail and mountain races — climbing strength, technical descent, and variable-pace endurance.
**Technical signature**: `trail / mountain race prep · maintenance to slight surplus · vertical work + technical + endurance · 12–20 weeks · deadline-bound · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: Runner training for trail races, mountain ultras, or vertical-K events. Differs from road running in three ways: significant vertical gain, technical terrain (variable pace, foot placement, descent control), and longer durations at lower paces. Established running base required (10+ km comfortable); ideally some hiking or vertical experience.
**Physiological definition**: Trail and mountain performance demands aerobic capacity plus lower-body strength for sustained climbing, eccentric strength for descent (quad-loading on downhills), and proprioceptive ability for technical sections. Pacing is variable rather than steady. Substrate utilization matters more than in road racing — events are longer, fueling is harder logistically, and fat oxidation efficiency directly affects performance.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance during base, surplus during peak training weeks
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight (eccentric load + recovery demand)
Carbohydrates 5–7 g/kg, higher around long days
Practice race-day nutrition with portable formats: bars, gels, real food
Hydration scale to climate (heat especially)
**Dominant training type**: Easy aerobic on trail (70–80% of volume) + 1× threshold/tempo (uphill repeats or tempo on rolling terrain) + 1× long run with vertical gain. Strength work 1–2× weekly emphasizing posterior chain (RDL, hip thrust), eccentric work for descents (Bulgarian split squat with controlled descent, depth jumps later in block), and core stability. Hiking with poles incorporated for ultras.
**Typical duration**: 12–20 weeks depending on race distance. 12 weeks for sub-marathon trail; 18–20 weeks for ultras.
**Frequency recommendation**: 4–6 runs/week + 1–2 strength + 0–1 hike. Weekly running volume varies by experience (35–80 km), but vertical gain is the more relevant load metric (1000–3000+ m/week at peak).
**Progress markers**:
Sustained climbing pace at controlled HR (fixed grade, fixed HR, faster speed)
Descent control: technical sections at race pace without quad failure
Long-run vertical gain progressing
Recovery between long days improving
Resting HR and HRV stable across weeks
**Common pitfalls**:
Training only on flat: race terrain is the specific stimulus, road volume doesn't transfer fully
Neglecting descent practice: most race injuries and quad failures happen on downhills
Skipping strength: trail running breaks down lower-body structure faster than road
Underestimating fueling: longer durations + harder logistics = more fueling failures
Comparing road pace expectations to trail pace: irrelevant comparison
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health (especially ankle and hip) · General strength (low volume) · Cardiovascular health focus
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Other race prep goals · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Koop, J., Rutberg, J. Training Essentials for Ultrarunning (VeloPress, 2016).
Hoffman, M. (2010). Performance trends in 161-km ultramarathons. Int J Sports Med.
Vernillo, G. et al. (2017). Biomechanics and physiology of uphill and downhill running. Sports Med.
Millet, G., Millet, G.P. (2012). Ultramarathon is an outstanding model for the study of adaptive responses to extreme load and stress. BMC Med.
Magness, S. The Science of Running (2014).
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Target trail race completed at target time OR target elevation total reached in training (e.g., 5000m cumulative vertical in 4-week block) plus longest technical session completed without injury. Strength held through block.
*Window*: Single-test = race day, OR cumulative weekly elevation tracked over 4-6 weeks for non-racing users.
*Next step*: Recovery week, then maintenance trail running, next race, or shift to road C1/C2 or D-cluster.
*Detection*: Passive — elevation gain log (GPS), session distance, race import. Prompted post-key-session: "Technical sections — comfortable, on-edge, or sketchy?" Plus post-session checkbox: "Was this a race-simulation?" (flags practice technical sessions or simulation long-runs as event-grade for readiness confirmation).

entries.heading: C4 · Hybrid athlete (Hyrox-style)
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for hybrid races — Hyrox, DekaFit, similar — with concurrent strength, work capacity, and running.
**Technical signature**: `hybrid race prep · maintenance kcal · concurrent strength + endurance + running · 12–16 weeks · deadline-bound or open-ended · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: Athlete training for Hyrox or similar hybrid events: alternating running segments with functional strength stations (sled push/pull, burpee broad jumps, sandbag carries, wall balls, etc.). Also fits anyone wanting "fitness across the board" without picking pure strength or pure endurance — but for that user the technical signature is the existing Hybrid Athletic Training Doctrine, not race-specific.
**Physiological definition**: Hybrid performance demands concurrent adaptation across strength, work capacity (strength endurance under sustained metabolic stress), aerobic capacity (running base), and movement economy under fatigue. Interference between strength and endurance exists but is manageable when sessions are sequenced correctly: heavy strength and HIIT separated by 6+ hours, Zone 2 not stacked on heavy strength days. The full Hybrid Athletic Training Doctrine (Manual + Framework + Plan + Protocol) operationalizes this for a 12-week block.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance, slight deficit (−10%) only during fat-oriented mesocycles
Protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates high on hard days, moderate on easy days
Hydration and sleep are non-negotiable given the training load
**Dominant training type**: Full Hybrid Athletic Training Doctrine: 4–5 strength sessions/week (Layer 1 templates) + 2–3 conditioning sessions/week (Zone 2 dominant + 1× tempo or HIIT). Mesocycle structure (per Plan Q1 2026):
	Weeks 1–4 Metabolic Foundation: aerobic base + fat oxidation
	Weeks 5–8 Structural Hypertrophy: lower-body growth + work capacity
	Weeks 9–12 Hybrid Integration: race-specific work + taper
For Hyrox specifically, race-specific stations practiced 1–2× weekly in final 6 weeks.
**Typical duration**: 12–16 weeks per block. Open-ended outside race windows (the doctrine sustains long-term).
**Frequency recommendation**: 5 sessions/week per Layer 5 Coupling Logic: Mon Lower Post · Tue Upper · Thu Lower Ant · Fri Mobility · Sat Full Body. Adjustable to 4-day for shorter weeks.
**Progress markers**:
Strength maintained on RDL, squat, press, row across the block
HR drift in Zone 2 <5%
ROM improving (mobility integration succeeding)
Race-pace simulation: full Hyrox sequence completed within target time in final 4 weeks
Recovery (sleep, HRV) stable
**Common pitfalls**:
Trying to peak strength and endurance simultaneously: pick a primary
Skipping mobility: Hybrid load accumulates joint stress; mobility is the relief valve
Going too hard on Zone 2: it's recovery work, not training stimulus
Neglecting race-specific stations: Hyrox isn't won purely on strength + running
Stacking HIIT on heavy strength days: violates Layer 2 doctrine
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · Strength endurance · Cardiovascular health focus · Glute development at low intensity
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Major weight loss · Race prep — short / long distance
**Sources**:
Hybrid Athletic Training Manual, Framework, Plan, Protocol (internal doctrine — see KB hierarchy).
Coffey, V., Hawley, J. (2017). Concurrent exercise training: Do opposites distract? J Physiol.
Wilson, J. et al. (2012). Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises. J Strength Cond Res.
Methenitis, S. (2018). A brief review on concurrent training: from laboratory to the field. Sports.
Mangine, G. et al. (2020). Crossfit-based high intensity power training improves maximal aerobic fitness and body composition. J Strength Cond Res.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Hyrox event completed at target time, OR practice-event simulation hit target time. Strength markers maintained (key compounds) AND endurance markers reached (run pace, row split, sled push capacity).
*Window*: Single-test on event day, OR 2-week practice-event confirmation.
*Next step*: Recovery + transition to next Hyrox cycle (with focus rotation), or shift to strength-emphasis (B1) or pure endurance (C1-C3) block.
*Detection*: Passive — event time, station splits. Prompted at midpoint: "Are weak stations identifiable?" (routes focus for next 4 weeks). Plus post-session checkbox: "Was this a race-simulation?" (distinguishes practice-event simulations from regular sessions for marker confirmation).

entries.heading: C5 · Cycling event prep
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for a sportive, gran fondo, or stage event — aerobic base, climbing power, and event-specific endurance.
**Technical signature**: `cycling event prep · maintenance to slight surplus · aerobic + threshold + climbing + event-specific · 12–20 weeks · deadline-bound · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: Cyclist training for a sportive (organized long-distance ride), gran fondo, multi-day stage event, or first century. Established cycling base preferred (3+ months riding consistently). Differs from running events in lower joint impact (allows higher weekly volume) and equipment dependence (bike fit, gearing, pacing tools matter).
**Physiological definition**: Cycling performance is dominated by aerobic capacity, lactate threshold (or FTP — Functional Threshold Power), and event-specific demands (sustained climbs, repeated surges, all-day endurance). Power-based training (watts) provides cleaner load tracking than heart rate alone, especially for threshold and VO2max work. Polarized model (80/20) applies as in running. Climbing-specific work is essential for mountainous events.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance during base, slight surplus during peak weeks
Protein 1.6–1.8 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates 6–10 g/kg on training days, very high around long rides
On-bike fueling 60–90 g carb/hour during long rides — practice in training
Hydration scaled to climate and ride duration
**Dominant training type**: Easy aerobic (Zone 2, 70–80% of volume) + 1× threshold/sweet-spot session + 1× long ride weekly. Hill intervals 1–2× per block for climbing-heavy events. Strength work 1–2× weekly (squat, RDL, single-leg work) for power production and injury resilience. Tapering 1–2 weeks before event.
**Typical duration**: 12–20 weeks. Stage-event prep on the longer end (more accumulation, more recovery, more race-specific volume).
**Frequency recommendation**: 4–5 rides/week + 1–2 strength sessions. Weekly volume scales with experience: 6–10 hours (entry sportive), 10–15 hours (advanced events).
**Progress markers**:
FTP (or threshold pace) rising over the block
Easy ride HR dropping at fixed power (aerobic adaptation)
Long ride distance progressing
Climbing power sustaining longer at threshold
Ride-day fueling tolerated without GI issues
**Common pitfalls**:
Too much sweet-spot, not enough easy: middle-zone training without polarization plateaus quickly
Neglecting strength: power production and injury resilience both suffer
Skipping bike fit: chronic knee/back/neck issues nearly always trace to fit
Training without on-bike fueling practice: event-day GI failures common
Junk miles: low-quality time on the bike accumulates fatigue without adaptation
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health (hip and thoracic spine especially) · General strength (low volume) · Cardiovascular health focus · Sustainable fat loss only at very mild deficit and only outside peak training weeks
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Other race prep goals · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Allen, H., Coggan, A., McGregor, S. Training and Racing with a Power Meter (3rd ed., VeloPress, 2019).
Friel, J. The Cyclist's Training Bible (5th ed., VeloPress, 2018).
Seiler, S. (2010). What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
Burke, L. et al. (2011). Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci.
Rønnestad, B., Mujika, I. (2014). Optimizing strength training for running and cycling endurance performance. Scand J Med Sci Sports.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Event completed at target time/power. FTP test at week -3 confirmed target. Long ride progression hit peak distance. Strength held per plan.
*Window*: Single-test = event. FTP test week -3 as primary readiness indicator.
*Next step*: Recovery week, then maintenance cycling, next event block, or shift to other goal.
*Detection*: Passive — power data (if available), FTP test result, long ride logs, event result. Prompted post-event: "Pacing on target or detonated?" Plus post-session checkbox: "Was this a race-simulation?" (flags practice events or simulation rides as event-grade for peak-readiness confirmation).

entries.heading: C6 · Combat sports prep
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Support your fight-prep camp — strength, conditioning, and injury prevention to complement your sport-specific training.
**Technical signature**: `combat sports S&C · maintenance kcal (or weight-cut adjusted) · strength + power + conditioning · 8–12 week camps · primary or compatible-secondary to sport practice`
**Who picks this**: Athlete in BJJ, boxing, MMA, Muay Thai, wrestling, or judo running a fight camp or competition prep. The KB does not replace sport-specific technical training — it complements it as the strength & conditioning layer. Most users in this category will run sport practice as the primary load and S&C as the supporting structure.
**Physiological definition**: Combat performance demands strength-power across the body, repeat-bout work capacity (high-intensity efforts with brief recovery), aerobic base for sustained rounds, grip and core strength for grappling sports, and injury resilience under contact load. Sport practice is the irreplaceable primary stimulus; the S&C layer manages residual fatigue while building force, power, and capacity that the sport itself doesn't develop directly.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance during camp; weight-cut adjustments managed separately and ideally with professional supervision (rapid weight cutting carries health and performance risks)
Protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates high on hard sport days, moderate on lighter days
Hydration is critical given combat sports' often sub-optimal recovery rhythms
**Dominant training type**: 2–3× S&C sessions/week alongside sport practice. Heavy compounds (squat, deadlift, bench, press) maintained at low-volume / moderate-intensity for force; explosive work (cleans, jumps, medicine ball throws, sprints) for power; specific conditioning (sled, rower intervals, prowler) matched to round duration. Strength endurance work 1× weekly. Conditioning logic per Layer 2 (max 3×/week) but combat sports often exceed that via sport practice — the KB's job is to integrate, not duplicate.
**Typical duration**: 8–12 weeks per fight camp. Off-camp blocks run general strength + conditioning to maintain capacity.
**Frequency recommendation**: 2–3 S&C sessions + 4–6 sport practice sessions/week during camp. Total weekly load is high; recovery is the binding constraint. Reduce S&C volume sharply if sport practice intensity rises.
**Progress markers**:
Force production maintained or rising on key compounds
Power output (jump height, throw distance, sprint times) rising
Repeat-bout capacity: less HR rise across rounds, faster recovery between
Sport-specific markers: round endurance, output sustained late in fights
Recovery (sleep, HRV) stable; deterioration signals overload
**Common pitfalls**:
Treating S&C like bodybuilding: high volume + soreness compete with sport practice
Adding HIIT on top of sport conditioning: violates Layer 2, accumulates fatigue
Aggressive weight cuts without supervision: performance and health risks
Skipping deload weeks during long camps: chronic overreach common
Neglecting grip and neck work for grappling sports: silent weak points
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · Strength endurance · Cardiovascular health focus · Sustainable fat loss only outside camp blocks
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Race prep (any distance) · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Turner, A. et al. (2019). Strength and conditioning for combat sports. Strength Cond J.
Reale, R. et al. (2017). Acute weight loss strategies for combat sports. Sports Med.
Slimani, M. et al. (2017). Effects of plyometric training on physical fitness in team sport athletes: a systematic review. J Hum Kinet.
James, L. et al. (2016). Periodization for mixed martial arts. Strength Cond J.
McGuigan, M. Monitoring Training and Performance in Athletes (Human Kinetics, 2017).
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Fight/competition completed (regardless of outcome — completion is the marker for non-elite). Strength/conditioning markers held through camp. Weight cut executed cleanly if applicable (within 24h re-hydration).
*Window*: Single-test = competition day. Mid-camp readiness check at week -4.
*Next step*: Extended recovery (mental as well as physical), debrief week, then either next camp prep or off-season base building.
*Detection*: Passive — strength logs, conditioning test (e.g., 2km row, 5min max effort). Prompted post-event: "Recovery type needed — full off-week, light maintenance, or quick turnaround?" Plus post-session checkbox: "Was this a race-simulation / sparring at competition intensity?" (distinguishes competition-grade work from regular training).

entries.heading: C7 · Racquet sports
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Support tennis, padel, or squash — rotational power, lateral movement, and recovery between points.
**Technical signature**: `racquet sports S&C · maintenance kcal · rotational power + agility + repeat-bout · 8–12 weeks (in-season) or 12–16 weeks (off-season) · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Recreational or competitive tennis, padel, or squash player wanting to add S&C structure alongside their on-court time. As with combat sports, on-court practice is the primary stimulus; S&C complements it.
**Physiological definition**: Racquet sport performance demands rotational power (hips and torso, transferring through the racquet), repeat-sprint capacity (short intense efforts with brief recovery between points), lateral agility and change-of-direction speed, and shoulder/elbow durability under repeated overhead loads. Single-leg strength and unilateral stability matter more than bilateral max strength. Energy system: alactic and lactic intervals dominate; aerobic base supports recovery between points and sets.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.6–1.8 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates moderate to high (especially around match days and high-volume practice)
Hydration scaled to climate and match length
**Dominant training type**: 2–3× S&C sessions/week during in-season; 3–4× during off-season. Rotational work (medicine ball throws, cable rotations, landmine work), unilateral lower-body strength (BSS, single-leg RDL, lunges), shoulder durability (band work, scapular control, rotator cuff), and short-interval conditioning. Plyometrics for change-of-direction speed.
**Typical duration**:
In-season: 8–12 weeks of maintenance-flavored S&C
Off-season: 12–16 weeks of strength-and-power building before tournament season
**Frequency recommendation**: In-season: 2× S&C + 3–5 court sessions. Off-season: 3–4× S&C + 2–3 court sessions.
**Progress markers**:
Rotational power output (medicine ball throw distance) rising
Lateral acceleration (5–10m timed shuttles) faster
Single-leg strength (BSS, single-leg squat) progressing
Shoulder mobility and stability stable; pain absent
Match-end fatigue: later onset, less drop-off
**Common pitfalls**:
Bilateral squat focus only: court sport is unilateral; transfer is limited
Skipping shoulder durability work: rotator cuff and elbow injuries common in racquet sports
High-volume cardio: irrelevant for the sport's energy system, steals from recovery
No rotational work: neglects the primary force expression of the sport
Neglecting single-leg eccentrics: lateral movement injuries (knee, ankle) often trace here
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health (especially hip rotation and shoulder) · General strength · Cardiovascular health focus
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk (during competition phases) · Race prep — long distance · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Reid, M., Schneiker, K. (2008). Strength and conditioning in tennis: current research and practice. J Sci Med Sport.
Kovacs, M. (2007). Tennis physiology: training the competitive athlete. Sports Med.
Girard, O., Millet, G. (2009). Physical determinants of tennis performance in competitive teenage players. J Strength Cond Res.
Turner, A., Stewart, P. (2014). Strength and conditioning for soccer players. Strength Cond J.
Ellenbecker, T., Roetert, E. (2002). Effects of a 4-month season on glenohumeral joint rotational strength and range of motion in female collegiate tennis players. J Strength Cond Res.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Tournament/match goal achieved (rating/ranking reached, specific opponent beaten, league position) OR off-court performance markers reached (shoulder endurance test, lateral agility test, rotational power test).
*Window*: Match-day single-test OR rolling 4-week tournament results, depending on user goal phrasing.
*Next step*: Transition to off-season strength/mobility block, or continue in-season maintenance, or shift to recovery.
*Detection*: Passive — strength/agility test logs. Prompted post-tournament: "Body holding up over multi-day play, or breaking down?" Plus post-session checkbox: "Was this a race-simulation / tournament-grade match?" (flags competition-grade practice from regular training).

entries.heading: C8 · Climbing / bouldering
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Build climbing strength — pulling power, finger conditioning, antagonist balance, and mobility for hard moves.
**Technical signature**: `climbing/bouldering S&C · maintenance kcal · pull strength + finger + antagonist + mobility · 8–16 weeks · primary or compatible-secondary to climbing practice`
**Who picks this**: Climber or boulderer training to push grades or recover from plateau. Climbing practice on the wall is the primary skill stimulus; the KB layer provides the strength, conditioning, and antagonist balance that climbing alone underdevelops or imbalances. Best for climbers with at least 6+ months of regular climbing — pure beginners gain more from climbing time than supplementary work.
**Physiological definition**: Climbing performance demands relative strength (force per unit body weight), finger and forearm conditioning (specific to crimps, slopers, pinches), pulling strength across multiple shoulder angles, antagonist development (push muscles, often underdeveloped relative to pull), core stability for body tension, and shoulder/hip mobility for hard movement. Hangboard and campus board work develop finger and contact strength specifically; lifted strength work develops the muscular force the fingers transmit.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance — climbing rewards relative strength, but cuts impair finger recovery
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates moderate; sufficient around hard climbing sessions
Sleep is especially important: finger tendons and pulleys recover slowly
**Dominant training type**: Climbing practice (3–5×/week) as primary stimulus. Supplementary S&C 1–2×/week:
Hangboard protocols (max hangs or repeaters) when progressing finger strength
Pull work (weighted pull-ups, lock-offs, one-arm progressions) for absolute strength
Antagonist work (push press, dips, rows, scapular control) for shoulder balance
Core stability (front lever progressions, hanging leg raises, anti-rotation)
Mobility (hip openers, shoulder flexion, internal rotation)
Hangboard and high-intensity finger work are skill-adjacent — done fresh, never to failure, recovery between attempts >3 minutes. Apply Layer 2.5 GTG logic.
**Typical duration**: 8–12 weeks for grade-pushing block, 12–16 weeks for project-specific prep (e.g. an outdoor sending trip).
**Frequency recommendation**: Climbing 3–5×/week + 1–2× S&C. Hangboard separate from climbing days when possible to keep finger stimulus fresh.
**Progress markers**:
Hangboard progression: holding more weight at fixed edge size, or smaller edge at fixed weight
Pull strength: weighted pull-up max rising
Antagonist balance: push:pull ratio improving toward 1:1.5
Mobility: hip flexion and shoulder flexion improving
Climbing grade: project-level send rate rising
Finger and elbow tendons: pain-free across the block
**Common pitfalls**:
Hangboarding too frequently: fingers don't recover like muscles — 2× weekly is the ceiling for most
Neglecting antagonists: chronic anterior shoulder pain and elbow issues
Cutting calories during heavy climbing: finger injury risk rises
Hangboarding before climbing time: backwards skill priority (climb first when fresh, hangboard after or on separate days)
Ignoring mobility: hip and shoulder restrictions limit grade ceiling more than strength does for many climbers
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health (especially hip and shoulder) · General strength (low volume) · Sustainable fat loss only at very mild deficit
**Incompatible goals**: Build muscle / lean bulk · Strength peak · Race prep — long distance · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Saul, D. et al. (2019). Determinants for success in climbing: a systematic review. J Exerc Sci Fit.
López-Rivera, E., González-Badillo, J. (2019). Comparison of the effects of three hangboard strength and endurance training programs on grip endurance in sport climbers. J Hum Kinet.
Hörst, E. Training for Climbing (3rd ed., Falcon Guides, 2016).
MacLeod, D. 9 Out of 10 Climbers Make the Same Mistakes (Rare Breed Productions, 2010).
Mundry, S. et al. (2021). Hangboard training in advanced climbers: a randomized controlled trial. Sci Rep.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Target grade sent (e.g., V6 boulder, 7a route) clean, repeated, on more than one route/problem. Hangboard target reached (e.g., 7-second one-arm hang, 20mm edge for advanced; appropriately scaled for level).
*Window*: Send confirmation = 2+ clean sends on different problems at the grade. Hangboard target sustained over 2 sessions.
*Next step*: Project next grade, transition to volume/endurance phase, or off-wall strength block.
*Detection*: Passive — grade log, hangboard time/load log. Prompted post-send: "Felt at limit, or with room?" (routes next progression decision).

entries.heading: C9 · Team sport season prep
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for football, basketball, soccer, hockey, or similar — off-season build, in-season maintenance, with sport-specific demands.
**Technical signature**: `team sport S&C · maintenance kcal · strength + power + repeat-sprint · phased by season · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Athlete playing a team sport (football/soccer, basketball, hockey, rugby, lacrosse, American football, etc.) wanting periodized S&C aligned with the sport's seasonal structure. Differs from individual sports because the competition calendar is largely fixed, training adapts around match congestion, and position-specific demands vary widely (e.g. soccer center-back vs winger).
**Physiological definition**: Team sports demand strength-power, repeat-sprint capacity (short maximal efforts with brief recovery, sustained over 60–90+ minute matches), agility and change of direction, position-specific endurance, and durability under collision/contact load. Energy systems span all three (alactic for sprints, lactic for sustained efforts, aerobic for recovery between bouts). Periodization splits the year into off-season (build), pre-season (specificity), in-season (maintenance + recovery), and transition.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance during season; surplus during off-season hypertrophy phases
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates high on match days and 1–2 days prior; moderate on training days
Hydration and recovery nutrition prioritized given match-density
**Dominant training type**: Phased by season:
*Off-season (8–12 weeks)*: Strength + hypertrophy emphasis (compound lifts, 6–10 reps, RPE 7–8). Aerobic base build via Zone 2. Plyometric and sprint work introduced in second half.
*Pre-season (4–6 weeks)*: Strength shifts toward power (low-rep heavy lifts + explosive work). Conditioning becomes sport-specific (repeat-sprint protocols, change-of-direction work). Match-specific volume rises.
*In-season (variable, often 6+ months)*: Maintenance strength (1–2× weekly, low volume / high intensity to preserve gains). Recovery work and mobility prioritized between matches. No new stimulus during high match-density weeks.
*Transition (2–4 weeks)*: Active rest, mobility, low-stress activity.
**Typical duration**: Year-round periodization. Each phase has its own length per the sport's calendar.
**Frequency recommendation**:
Off-season 4× S&C/week
Pre-season 3× S&C + 4–5× sport practice/week
In-season 1–2× S&C + 4–6× sport practice + matches
**Progress markers**:
Strength maintained or rising during season (drop signals overload)
Sprint times stable or improving
Vertical jump / power output stable through season
Match-end fatigue: later onset, less drop-off
Injury rate low (most concrete marker of well-managed S&C)
Recovery markers (HRV, sleep) stable across match weeks
**Common pitfalls**:
High-volume strength in-season: undermines match performance and recovery
Neglecting in-season strength entirely: significant strength loss across a 6-month season
Pre-season "fitness tests" without build: injury cluster in week 1
Generic conditioning ignoring position demands: midfielders ≠ defenders ≠ forwards
Skipping transition weeks: chronic overreach across years
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General strength (off-season) · Cardiovascular health focus · Combat sports prep (rare overlap, similar S&C principles)
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk (in-season) · Race prep (any distance) · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Bishop, D. et al. (2008). Repeated-sprint ability — Part I: factors contributing to fatigue. Sports Med.
Gabbett, T. (2016). The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med.
Bompa, T., Buzzichelli, C. Periodization: Theory and Methodology of Training (6th ed., 2018).
Turner, A., Stewart, P. (2014). Strength and conditioning for soccer players. Strength Cond J.
Suchomel, T. et al. (2018). The importance of muscular strength: training considerations. Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Pre-season readiness markers reached (sprint test, agility test, conditioning test all at target). Season starts injury-free. In-season: maintenance of those markers through the season's high points.
*Window*: Pre-season block end = single-test readiness suite. In-season = rolling 4-week monitoring.
*Next step*: Transition to in-season maintenance mode, post-season recovery, or off-season base block.
*Detection*: Passive — test result logs, session loads. Prompted weekly in-season: "Energy and recovery on track?"

entries.heading: D1 · General health maintenance
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Stay strong, mobile, and healthy long-term — without chasing a specific performance or physique goal.
**Technical signature**: `general health · maintenance kcal · balanced strength + Zone 2 + mobility · open-ended · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Someone who wants to keep training without a specific objective: maintain strength, cardiovascular health, and mobility across years. Often the chosen goal between performance blocks, after reaching a target, or as a baseline for someone whose primary focus is not training-driven (career, family, life phase). Distinct from "Maintenance / recovery week" in Layer 5 — that's a 1–2 week structural recovery, this is an ongoing operating mode.
**Physiological definition**: Sustained moderate training stimulus across strength (preserves muscle, bone density, neural function), aerobic conditioning (cardiovascular health, metabolic flexibility), and mobility (joint range, fall prevention, movement quality). Volumes are moderate — enough to drive adaptation against detraining, low enough to remain sustainable indefinitely. Recovery exceeds training stress under all circumstances.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.4–1.8 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates and fats balanced per personal preference and dietary pattern
No specific tactics required beyond general dietary quality
**Dominant training type**: 3–4× strength sessions/week (full-body or upper/lower split), 2× Zone 2 conditioning, daily mobility (10–15 min). Strength volume held at MEV–MAV range. Conditioning sessions never to depletion.
**Typical duration**: Open-ended. Designed to run indefinitely or until user transitions to a directional goal.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3–4 sessions/week minimum. 5+ acceptable if recovery sustains it. Below 3 sessions/week, gains slowly erode.
**Progress markers**:
Strength on key compounds maintained or slowly rising
Cardiovascular markers: resting HR stable, HR drift in Zone 2 <5%
Mobility: ROM holding across years
Sleep, mood, energy stable
Body composition stable
Subjective wellbeing high (the most relevant marker for this goal)
**Common pitfalls**:
Drifting to under-stimulus over months: 2× weekly without progression eventually equals detraining
Adding random "challenges" that disrupt the maintenance pattern: derails what's working
Skipping the goal entirely between performance blocks: detraining costs more recovery later
Treating it as "just exercise": structure still matters — random training produces random outcomes
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · Cardiovascular health focus · Bone density · Metabolic health · Single-area aesthetic at low intensity
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Garber, C. et al. (2011). American College of Sports Medicine position stand: quantity and quality of exercise for developing and maintaining cardiorespiratory, musculoskeletal, and neuromotor fitness in apparently healthy adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc.
WHO (2020). Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. World Health Organization.
Lee, I. et al. (2012). Effect of physical inactivity on major non-communicable diseases worldwide. Lancet.
Booth, F. et al. (2017). Lack of exercise is a major cause of chronic diseases. Compr Physiol.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: 12 weeks of consistent training (≥75% session completion), key health markers stable or improving (resting HR, sleep quality, energy self-report), strength baseline maintained, mobility baseline maintained.
*Window*: Rolling 12-week assessment; not a single-test goal.
*Next step*: Continue — D1 is an indefinite goal. If user wants directional change, route to specific goal (A1, B1, etc.) with D1 as compatible secondary.
*Detection*: Passive — session completion rate, strength/mobility logs, optional wearable data. Prompted quarterly: "Still on track with what you wanted from training?"

entries.heading: D2 · Cardiovascular health focus
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for heart health — cardiovascular conditioning leads, with strength supporting.
**Technical signature**: `cardiovascular health · maintenance kcal · Zone 2 dominant + strength supporting · open-ended · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Someone with cardiovascular health as the primary motivator: family history of heart disease, post-cardiac event (cleared by physician), elevated blood pressure, or simply prioritizing heart function as the lead training driver. Aerobic work dominates; strength supports without dominating.
**Physiological definition**: Cardiovascular adaptations include increased stroke volume, expanded mitochondrial density, improved capillary density, lower resting HR, improved blood pressure regulation, and enhanced metabolic flexibility. Zone 2 training drives these adaptations efficiently; higher-intensity work (Zone 4–5) provides additional VO2max stimulus but at higher recovery cost. The combination, polarized 80/20, produces the broadest adaptation.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.4–1.8 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates moderate to high; fuel matches conditioning load
Fats emphasize unsaturated, omega-3 priority
Mediterranean-pattern eating maps well onto cardiovascular focus
**Dominant training type**: 3–4× Zone 2 conditioning weekly (45–60 min) + 1× tempo or interval session + 2–3× strength sessions (compounds, moderate volume). Mobility daily for joint maintenance.
**Typical duration**: Open-ended. Cardiovascular adaptations consolidate over 12+ weeks; long-term sustained training compounds them.
**Frequency recommendation**: Conditioning 4–5×/week + 2–3× strength. Zone 2 sessions can be walking, cycling, swimming, low-impact rowing — modality flexibility is high.
**Progress markers**:
Resting HR dropping over months
Blood pressure improving (if elevated)
HR drift in Zone 2 <5% within session
VO2max (estimated or measured) rising
HR recovery 1 minute post-effort improving
Subjective endurance in daily activity improving
**Common pitfalls**:
Replacing all strength with cardio: muscle loss reduces metabolic rate and hurts long-term cardiovascular health
Going too hard on Zone 2: defeats the purpose; HR target is 70–75% HRmax, conversational pace
Neglecting strength: leg strength predicts longevity and cardiac function more strongly than aerobic markers in older populations
Cardio-only programs that ignore mobility: joint stiffness limits volume long-term
