**Compatible secondary goals**: General health maintenance · Metabolic health · Mobility & joint health · Sustainable fat loss only at very mild deficit
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Race prep — long distance · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Lavie, C. et al. (2015). Exercise and the cardiovascular system: clinical science and cardiovascular outcomes. Circ Res.
Whelton, P. et al. (2018). 2017 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure. J Am Coll Cardiol.
Kodama, S. et al. (2009). Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women. JAMA.
Pelliccia, A. et al. (2021). 2020 ESC Guidelines on sports cardiology and exercise in patients with cardiovascular disease. Eur Heart J.
Seiler, S. (2010). What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? Int J Sports Physiol Perform.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Resting HR improved by ≥5 bpm OR HRV trending up over 12-week window. Zone 2 capacity improved (longer duration at same HR, or lower HR at same pace). Recovery markers (sleep, RHR) consistent.
*Window*: 12-week rolling window; primary metrics tracked weekly.
*Next step*: Continue at maintenance, OR shift to endurance event prep (C1-C5), OR add strength emphasis (B1) as compatible secondary.
*Detection*: Passive — wearable HR data, Zone 2 session pace/HR logs. Prompted at week 12: "Notice the change in resting feel?"

entries.heading: D3 · Metabolic health
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for blood-sugar regulation, insulin sensitivity, and metabolic resilience — for users with pre-diabetes, type 2 diabetes (post-clearance), or family history.
**Technical signature**: `metabolic health · maintenance to slight deficit · resistance + Zone 2 priority · open-ended · medical-aware · primary or compatible-secondary`
⚠ **For users with diagnosed type 2 diabetes or pre-diabetes, recommend ongoing care with their physician.** Exercise affects blood glucose meaningfully and may require medication adjustments. The KB supplements clinical care, not replaces it.
**Who picks this**: Someone with pre-diabetes, type 2 diabetes (post-clearance), elevated fasting glucose or HbA1c, metabolic syndrome, or strong family history of these conditions. Also fits users prioritizing metabolic flexibility as a longevity marker.
**Physiological definition**: Resistance training increases muscle mass and glucose uptake capacity (skeletal muscle is the primary site for postprandial glucose disposal). Aerobic training improves insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial function, and substrate flexibility (the ability to switch between fat and carbohydrate as fuel). Combined resistance + aerobic training produces the strongest improvements in HbA1c and insulin sensitivity. Post-meal walks specifically blunt glucose excursions.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance to slight deficit (especially if BMI elevated)
Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg body weight
Carbohydrates moderate, distributed across meals; avoid large isolated boluses
Fiber emphasis (slows glucose absorption)
Mediterranean or moderate-carb pattern maps well
**Dominant training type**: 3× resistance training/week (compounds preferred — squat, deadlift, press, row, with hypertrophy-flavored rep ranges) + 2–3× Zone 2 conditioning. Post-meal walking (10–15 min) as additional metabolic tool. HIIT optional, 1× weekly maximum, well-spaced from heavy strength.
**Typical duration**: Open-ended. Metabolic adaptations show on labs within 8–12 weeks; long-term consistency drives durable change.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3 strength + 3 conditioning sessions/week + daily post-meal walks (5–15 min after main meals).
**Progress markers**:
HbA1c dropping over 12+ week windows (clinical lab)
Fasting glucose trending down
Continuous glucose monitor (if used): less variability, lower spikes
Resting HR dropping
Body weight and waist trending in goal direction
Strength rising (muscle mass is the metabolic protective tissue)
**Common pitfalls**:
Cardio-only programs: miss the muscle-mass driver of glucose disposal
Skipping post-meal movement: easy intervention, large effect on glucose excursions
Aggressive low-carb without medical oversight (for medication users): hypoglycemia risk
Going too hard, too often: cortisol elevation can worsen insulin resistance
Ignoring sleep: poor sleep raises insulin resistance independent of training
**Compatible secondary goals**: Cardiovascular health focus · General health maintenance · Sustainable fat loss · Major weight loss (often paired) · Mobility & joint health
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk (during deficit phases) · Race prep — long distance · Body recomposition
**Sources**:
Colberg, S. et al. (2016). Physical activity/exercise and diabetes: a position statement of the American Diabetes Association. Diabetes Care.
Davies, M. et al. (2022). Management of hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes, 2022. A consensus report by the ADA and EASD. Diabetes Care.
Pesta, D., Goncalves, R. (2017). Resistance training to improve type 2 diabetes: working toward a prescription for the future. Nutr Metab.
Buffey, A. et al. (2022). The acute effects of interrupting prolonged sitting time in adults with standing and light-intensity walking on biomarkers of cardiometabolic health: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med.
Reynolds, A. et al. (2016). Advice to walk after meals is more effective for lowering postprandial glycaemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus than advice that does not specify timing. Diabetologia.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Clinical markers improved (HbA1c, fasting glucose, lipid panel, blood pressure — where user shares results). Body composition improvements with metabolic-positive emphasis. Energy stability throughout day reported.
*Window*: Clinical markers per medical cycle (3-6 months). Daily energy self-report rolling 4-week.
*Next step*: Continue indefinitely OR transition to D1 if metabolic markers stable, OR specialist consultation if markers worsen.
*Detection*: Prompted (markers user-entered) — "Have you had recent bloodwork? Want to log results?" Passive — bodyweight, training adherence.

entries.heading: D4 · Bone density
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train to build and protect bone density — heavy compound lifting and impact, especially relevant for women 40+ and anyone with osteopenia.
**Technical signature**: `bone density · maintenance kcal · heavy resistance + impact · open-ended · medical-aware · primary or compatible-secondary`
⚠ **For users with diagnosed osteoporosis, prior fragility fracture, or recent imaging suggesting low bone density, recommend consultation with their physician before heavy loading.** The LIFTMOR trial demonstrated heavy lifting is safe and effective for postmenopausal women with low bone density when supervised — but starting protocols benefit from clinical context.
**Who picks this**: Women 40+ (peri- and postmenopausal) for whom bone density is a long-term concern, anyone with diagnosed osteopenia or osteoporosis (post-clearance), users with strong family history of osteoporosis or fragility fractures, men 60+ prioritizing bone health.
**Physiological definition**: Bone responds to mechanical loading — both heavy resistance (>80% 1RM in compound lifts) and impact (jumping, hopping, running). Light loading and aerobic work do not drive significant bone density gains. The LIFTMOR trial demonstrated postmenopausal women with low bone density gained density in spine and femoral neck through heavy lifting (deadlift, squat, overhead press at 80–85% 1RM, 5 sets of 5) plus weighted jumps — protocols once thought too risky for this population.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance (deficit during a bone-building phase is counterproductive)
Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg body weight
Calcium and vitamin D meet recommended daily intakes (food first, supplement if needed)
Adequate caloric intake matters: chronic low energy availability drives bone loss in any population
**Dominant training type**: 2–3× heavy compound resistance training/week — deadlift, squat, overhead press, bench press, row at 80–85% 1RM, 3–5 sets of 3–5 reps with full rest. Plus weighted jumping (hops, bounds, drop landings) progressing in volume — typically 10–50 contacts/session, 2–3×/week. Mobility and balance work daily (especially for older users where fall prevention matters as much as bone density).
**Typical duration**: Open-ended. Bone remodeling takes months; meaningful density change shows on DEXA over 6–12+ months of consistent training.
**Frequency recommendation**: 2–3 heavy strength sessions + 2× impact work + 1–2× general conditioning + daily mobility/balance.
**Progress markers**:
DEXA bone density (clinical, 12-month intervals)
Strength: 1–5RM rising on heavy compound lifts
Movement quality: heavy compounds executed without compensation
Balance: single-leg stance time stable or rising (fall prevention metric)
No fragility events
**Common pitfalls**:
Light-load training only: doesn't drive bone density adaptation
Avoiding deadlift and squat in postmenopausal women: based on outdated thinking; LIFTMOR shows safety with proper supervision
Skipping impact work: resistance alone misses the impact-loading adaptation
Inadequate calorie or calcium intake: undermines remodeling
Ignoring balance work: density gains matter less if falls happen
**Compatible secondary goals**: General health maintenance · General strength · Mobility & joint health · Menopause / perimenopause-aware training · Senior fitness (60+)
**Incompatible goals**: Race prep — long distance · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Watson, S. et al. (2018). High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women With Osteopenia and Osteoporosis: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial. J Bone Miner Res.
Kelley, G., Kelley, K., Tran, Z. (2002). Resistance training and bone mineral density in women: a meta-analysis of controlled trials. Am J Phys Med Rehabil.
Beck, B. et al. (2017). Exercise and Sports Science Australia (ESSA) position statement on exercise prescription for the prevention and management of osteoporosis. J Sci Med Sport.
Daly, R. et al. (2019). Exercise for the prevention of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women: an evidence-based guide to the optimal prescription. Braz J Phys Ther.
US Preventive Services Task Force (2018). Screening for Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures. JAMA.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: DEXA bone density measurement stable or improved at follow-up scan, OR proxy markers met (heavy compound lifts at target loads, impact work tolerated, no fracture/stress reaction events during block). For LIFTMOR protocol followers: target loads reached on deadlift, overhead press, jumping chin-up.
*Window*: DEXA scan annual or per medical schedule. Proxy markers rolling 12-week.
*Next step*: Continue indefinitely — bone density is a long-game goal. Annual review with healthcare provider.
*Detection*: Prompted (DEXA result entry) — "Any recent scans to log?" Passive — strength log against protocol targets.

entries.heading: D5 · Mobility & joint health
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for range of motion and joint resilience — for chronic stiffness, recurring tightness, or long-term joint health as the primary objective.
**Technical signature**: `mobility & joint health · maintenance kcal · loaded mobility + end-range strength + flow · open-ended · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Someone for whom restricted range of motion or chronic stiffness is the primary complaint — desk-worker hip stiffness, shoulder mobility limitations, "I can't squat to depth", "my back is always tight." Also fits users prioritizing mobility as a longevity strategy. Distinguishes from Layer 1 Mobility session (which is a tool used by many goals) — here mobility itself is the primary goal driving the program.
**Physiological definition**: Mobility is the controlled active range a joint can move through under load. Different from passive flexibility (someone else moves your limb) or static stretching (no neural control at end range). Trainable through loaded mobility (Cossack squat, Jefferson curl, deep ATG splits), end-range isometrics (30-second holds at maximum range), PAILs/RAILs (progressive angular isometric loading at the joint capsule), and skill-based flow practice. Strength under range translates to durable joint health.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.4–1.8 g/kg body weight
General dietary quality; no specific tactics
**Dominant training type**: 2–3× dedicated mobility sessions/week (40–60 min each: hips, thoracic spine, ankles, shoulders) + daily mobility flow (10–15 min) + 2–3× strength sessions/week with end-range loading emphasis (e.g. ATG split squats, Jefferson curls, Cossack squats, deep overhead work). Conditioning moderate (1–2× Zone 2/week).
**Typical duration**: Open-ended. Range improvements of 10%+ at fixed joints typically appear over 12+ weeks of consistent loaded work.
**Frequency recommendation**: Mobility daily (some duration) + 2–3 dedicated longer sessions weekly + 2–3 strength sessions/week with end-range integration.
**Progress markers**:
Hip flexion / extension / abduction ROM rising
Shoulder flexion + thoracic extension rising
Ankle dorsiflexion (knee-to-wall test) progressing
Loaded mobility positions achievable: deep ATG split, Cossack to floor, Jefferson curl below knee
Subjective stiffness dropping
No mobility-related pain across the block
**Common pitfalls**:
Static stretching only: limited adaptation, doesn't transfer to active range
Skipping the loaded component: ROM without strength is fragile
Treating mobility as a finisher: the goal-version of mobility deserves dedicated sessions
Ignoring upstream/downstream restrictions: chronic hip stiffness often has thoracic or ankle contributors
Rushing PAILs/RAILs progression: 30-second holds at full effort are demanding; build slowly
**Compatible secondary goals**: General strength (low–moderate volume) · General health maintenance · Cardiovascular health focus · Most rehab goals · Climbing / bouldering
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep — long distance · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Behm, D. et al. (2016). Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab.
Spina, A. Functional Range Conditioning System (Functional Anatomy Seminars) — PAILs/RAILs framework.
Page, P. (2012). Current concepts in muscle stretching for exercise and rehabilitation. Int J Sports Phys Ther.
Konrad, A. et al. (2019). Increases in passive properties of the muscle-tendon unit are not maintained over a 24-h period after eccentric exercise. Eur J Appl Physiol.
Thomas, E. et al. (2018). The relation between stretching typology and stretching duration: the effects on range of motion. Int J Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Target ROM reached on key joints (e.g., ankle dorsiflexion 40°, shoulder flexion overhead unrestricted, hip flexion to squat depth, thoracic rotation 45° each side). Pain-free movement reported across daily activities and training.
*Window*: ROM tests every 4 weeks; pain reporting weekly.
*Next step*: Maintain with reduced frequency, OR integrate as compatible secondary with new primary goal.
*Detection*: Passive — mobility session logs. Prompted at week 8: "Daily activities feel different — easier, same, or worse?" Prompted at week 12: ROM self-test guided.

sections.heading: E · Rehabilitation
sections.content_markdown: *Each entry assumes the user has been cleared by a qualified physiotherapist or physician for resistance training. The KB does NOT replace clinical care — it is the strength-and-conditioning layer that runs alongside or after clinical rehab. Pre-clearance pain, acute injuries, and undiagnosed pathology are out of scope.*

entries.heading: E1 · Knee rehab
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild knee strength and function after ACL reconstruction, meniscus surgery, or patellar tendinopathy — once cleared by your physiotherapist or surgeon.
**Technical signature**: `knee rehab post-clearance · maintenance kcal · progressive loading + neuromuscular control · 12–24+ weeks · medical-aware · primary-only initially`
⚠ **Post-clearance only.** This template assumes the user has been cleared for resistance training. The KB does NOT replace physiotherapy.
**Who picks this**: Someone post-clearance after ACL reconstruction (typically 6+ months post-op), meniscus repair or trim (timeline per surgeon), patellar tendinopathy (sub-acute or chronic), or post-arthroscopic procedures. Also suitable for chronic anterior knee pain that has been clinically assessed and cleared for loading.
**Physiological definition**: Knee rehab progresses through capacity rebuilding (rebuilding strength after detraining and surgery), neuromuscular control (single-leg stability, landing mechanics), then performance restoration (return to sport-relevant demands). Patellar tendinopathy specifically responds to heavy slow resistance training (Kongsgaard, Beyer protocols) — eccentric and concentric loading at moderate volume, not stretch-and-rest. The Cook-Purdam tendon continuum frames staging.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance (deficits impair tendon and tissue remodeling)
Protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight (collagen synthesis support)
Vitamin C and gelatin/collagen 15g, 30–60 min pre-loading session, may support tendon adaptation
Sleep critical for tissue remodeling
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (capacity rebuild, weeks 1–6 post-clearance)*: Bilateral leg press, leg extension, hamstring curl, light squat patterns. Sets of 8–12, RPE 5–7. Build basic capacity before single-leg load.
*Phase 2 (single-leg + control, weeks 6–12)*: Bulgarian split squat, single-leg RDL, step-ups, slow eccentric work. Begin landing mechanics drills. Sets of 6–10, RPE 6–8.
*Phase 3 (loading + plyometrics, weeks 12+)*: Heavy bilateral and single-leg lifts, low-amplitude jumps progressing to higher demands, sport-specific re-entry.
For patellar tendinopathy specifically: heavy slow resistance (3 sets of 4–8 reps, 6-second tempo, 3×/week) is first-line evidence-based protocol. Conditioning: Zone 2 cycling, swimming, or rowing maintained throughout (low knee impact).
**Typical duration**: 12–24+ weeks per phase progression. ACL return-to-sport often 9–12 months post-op total; the KB picks up at the 6-month mark for typical users.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3 lower-body strength sessions/week + 2–3 low-impact conditioning + daily mobility. Upper body trained as normal in parallel.
**Progress markers**:
Symmetry: single-leg strength approaching uninjured side (target >90% within 12+ weeks)
Pain at loading: stays at or below 3/10 during and 24h post (tendinopathy framework)
Hop tests: return to symmetry within 6 months (ACL context)
Quad and hamstring strength rising on hold-to-fail or 1RM-equivalent tests
Functional progress: walking, stairs, then jogging, then sport-specific work without pain spike
No swelling 24h post-session
**Common pitfalls**:
Progressing too fast after surgery: re-injury risk well-documented
Avoiding load entirely (rest-and-stretch model for tendinopathy): outdated, doesn't drive adaptation
Skipping single-leg work: bilateral strength can mask asymmetry
Returning to running before quad strength symmetry: ACL re-rupture cluster
Discontinuing rehab once "feels okay": symptom relief precedes tissue capacity by months
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General health maintenance · Cardiovascular health focus
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Race prep — long distance · Body recomposition
**Sources**:
Adams, D. et al. (2012; updated CPG 2018). Knee Stability and Movement Coordination Impairments: Knee Ligament Sprain. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther — APTA Clinical Practice Guideline.
Logerstedt, D. et al. (2017). Knee Pain and Mobility Impairments: Meniscal and Articular Cartilage Lesions. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther — APTA CPG.
Kongsgaard, M. et al. (2009). Corticosteroid injections, eccentric decline squat training and heavy slow resistance training in patellar tendinopathy. Scand J Med Sci Sports.
Cook, J., Purdam, C. (2009). Is tendon pathology a continuum? A pathology model to explain the clinical presentation of load-induced tendinopathy. Br J Sports Med.
Wiggins, A. et al. (2016). Risk of secondary injury in younger athletes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Am J Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Pain-free through full active ROM. Symmetry test passed (single-leg squat to 70° both sides; single-leg hop distance within 10% of uninvolved side). Strength tests symmetric within 10%. Cleared by physiotherapist if professional care involved.
*Window*: Two consecutive symmetry-test sessions clean (across 2-week window) AND 4+ weeks pain-free in daily activities.
*Next step*: Graduated return to sport-specific demands OR transition to maintenance with knee-friendly programming AND/OR return to primary goal under modified parameters.
*Detection*: Prompted weekly — "Pain today on 0-10 scale, where, when?" Prompted at milestone moments — guided symmetry self-test. Passive — strength logs (single-leg work).

entries.heading: E2 · Lower back rehab
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild back resilience after mechanical low back pain — once cleared by your physiotherapist or physician.
**Technical signature**: `lower back rehab post-clearance · maintenance kcal · stability + hip mobility + progressive loading · 12–24+ weeks · medical-aware · primary-only initially`
⚠ **Post-clearance only.** Acute or undiagnosed low back pain belongs with a clinician. Red flag symptoms (radiating pain past the knee, numbness, bowel/bladder changes, unexplained weight loss, night pain) require medical evaluation, not the KB.
**Who picks this**: Someone post-clearance with a history of mechanical low back pain (not radiculopathy, not red flag signs), recurrent episodes seeking durable resilience, post-rehab return to lifting, or chronic non-specific low back pain stable enough for graded exposure to load.
**Physiological definition**: Mechanical back resilience requires spinal stability (the trunk's ability to maintain neutral position under load — the McGill-style "stiffness"), hip mobility (so the spine isn't the relief valve for restricted hips), graded exposure to load (progressive loading rebuilds capacity that pain/inactivity erodes), and movement variability. NICE guidelines emphasize movement and exercise as the durable management strategy, not rest or passive interventions.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg body weight
Adequate sleep is non-negotiable (sleep deprivation amplifies pain perception independent of tissue state)
Stress management: psychosocial factors are well-documented contributors to chronic low back pain trajectories
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (stability + mobility, weeks 1–6 post-clearance)*: McGill big-3 (curl-up, side plank, bird-dog) for spinal endurance. Hip mobility (90/90, hip flexor work, hip rotation). Loaded carries. Glute activation.
*Phase 2 (loaded patterns, weeks 6–12)*: Goblet squat, hip thrust, kettlebell deadlift, push-pull patterns at moderate load. Reintroduce hinging at controlled load (RDL with light to moderate weight, kept neutral).
*Phase 3 (strength rebuild, weeks 12+)*: Conventional or trap-bar deadlift, back squat, bench, row at moderate-to-heavy load. Build full capacity.
Conditioning: walking is the primary recovery and capacity tool. Zone 2 walking or low-impact cardio throughout. Avoid prolonged sitting.
**Typical duration**: 12–24+ weeks. Pain-free progression varies enormously by user history.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3 strength sessions + daily walking + daily mobility (10–15 min). Upper body unaffected and trained normally.
**Progress markers**:
Pain during and post-loading stable or trending down
Loaded patterns tolerated: deadlift to bodyweight × 1, squat to bodyweight × 1, etc.
Carries: farmer's walk to half body weight per hand
McGill endurance tests: side plank, plank, biering-sorensen times rising
Hip mobility: hip rotation and extension improving
Subjective confidence in lifting rising
**Common pitfalls**:
Resting "until pain goes away": delays capacity rebuild, often worsens chronic course
Avoiding hinging permanently after acute episode: deconditioning the most important pattern for back resilience
Catastrophizing language reinforcement ("my back is broken"): pain neuroscience research shows language and beliefs shape pain trajectories
Skipping hip mobility: chronic hip restriction is a leading mechanical contributor
Returning to heavy load too fast: graded exposure is the principle
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General strength (eventual) · Cardiovascular health focus · General health maintenance
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
McGill, S. Low Back Disorders: Evidence-Based Prevention and Rehabilitation (3rd ed., Human Kinetics, 2015).
NICE (2016, updated 2020). Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s: assessment and management — NG59.
Saragiotto, B. et al. (2016). Motor control exercise for chronic non-specific low-back pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev.
Hayden, J. et al. (2021). Exercise therapy for chronic low back pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev.
O'Sullivan, P. et al. (2018). Cognitive Functional Therapy: an integrated behavioral approach for the targeted management of disabling low back pain. Phys Ther.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Pain-free in sitting, standing, walking, sleeping for 4+ consecutive weeks. McGill big-3 endurance test scores at functional levels (side plank 60+ sec both sides, modified curl-up endurance, bird-dog 8+/side without form break). Loaded hinge progression tolerated.
*Window*: 4-week symptom-free window minimum before declaring graduation.
*Next step*: Graduated return to general strength (B1) with back-aware programming. Hinge progression continues at maintenance frequency.
*Detection*: Prompted weekly — pain rating + functional capacity questions. Prompted at week 4: guided big-3 self-test. Passive — session logs.

entries.heading: E3 · Shoulder rehab
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild shoulder strength and control after rotator cuff issues, impingement, or instability — once cleared.
**Technical signature**: `shoulder rehab post-clearance · maintenance kcal · scapular control + cuff loading + progressive overhead · 12–20 weeks · medical-aware · primary-only initially`
⚠ **Post-clearance only.** Acute shoulder injury, persistent night pain, significant weakness, or undiagnosed shoulder issues require clinical evaluation.
**Who picks this**: Someone post-clearance with rotator cuff tendinopathy, post-rotator-cuff-repair (per surgeon timeline), subacromial pain syndrome, post-frozen-shoulder mobilization, or stable instability cleared for progressive loading.
**Physiological definition**: Shoulder rehab demands rotator cuff capacity (the deep stabilizers must hold the humeral head centered), scapular control (the scapula must move with the arm — dyskinesis is a major silent contributor), progressive loading (capacity rebuilds with mechanical stimulus, not rest), and overhead reintroduction in graded steps. Recent literature (Lewis, Littlewood) frames many "impingement" presentations as load-management problems responsive to progressive loading rather than structural fixes.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight
Sleep critical (shoulder pain is often sleep-disruptive, which amplifies the cycle)
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (cuff + scapula, weeks 1–6 post-clearance)*: Band external rotation, scapular wall slides, scapular push-ups, prone Y/T/W, light face pulls. Sub-maximal effort. Daily.
*Phase 2 (loaded patterns below shoulder height, weeks 6–10)*: Seated/supported rows, pulldowns, low-incline pressing, light dumbbell work. Build capacity at non-overhead angles.
*Phase 3 (overhead reintroduction, weeks 10+)*: Landmine press → seated overhead press with dumbbells → barbell overhead press at moderate load. Pull-up progressions when pain-free hanging tolerated.
Conditioning unaffected. Mobility daily for thoracic spine and shoulder ROM.
**Typical duration**: 12–20 weeks for full rehab. Post-rotator-cuff-repair often 6+ months total; the KB layer enters at the post-clearance loading phase.
**Frequency recommendation**: Daily cuff/scapular work (10 min) + 3× upper-body strength sessions/week + lower body trained normally.
**Progress markers**:
Pain during loading stable or dropping (3/10 ceiling during, no spike 24h post)
Cuff strength: external rotation strength rising
Scapular control: visible improvement on push-up, overhead motions
Overhead capacity returning to bodyweight overhead pressing, then loaded
Functional ROM: full overhead reach without compensation
Sleep improving (proxy for shoulder irritability dropping)
**Common pitfalls**:
Avoiding all overhead work permanently: deconditioning, doesn't address the issue
Pressing through pain: tendon irritation cycle
Skipping cuff and scapular work: bigger lifts mask the deeper weak points
Treating "impingement" as structural rather than load-management: outdated framing
Not reintroducing pull-ups: hanging and pulling load is part of full shoulder capacity
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General strength (lower body and trunk unaffected) · Cardiovascular health focus · General health maintenance
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Build muscle / lean bulk · Climbing / bouldering (until full overhead capacity) · Racquet sports (until overhead durability rebuilt)
**Sources**:
Lewis, J. (2016). Rotator cuff related shoulder pain: assessment, management and uncertainties. Man Ther.
Littlewood, C. et al. (2013). Exercise for rotator cuff tendinopathy: a systematic review. Physiotherapy.
Edwards, P. et al. (2016). Exercise rehabilitation in the non-operative management of rotator cuff tears: a review of the literature. Int J Sports Phys Ther.
Cools, A. et al. (2014). Rehabilitation of scapular dyskinesis: from the office worker to the elite overhead athlete. Br J Sports Med.
Kuhn, J. et al. (2013). Effectiveness of physical therapy in treating atraumatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears: a multicenter prospective cohort study. J Shoulder Elbow Surg.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Full pain-free ROM in flexion, abduction, external rotation. Strength symmetric within 10% (loaded external rotation, scaption, push-up capacity). Overhead patterns reintroduced without symptom return.
*Window*: 4+ weeks symptom-free under loaded overhead work.
*Next step*: Graduated return to pressing/pulling at full capacity OR transition to maintenance with shoulder-aware programming.
*Detection*: Prompted weekly — pain + functional task questions ("can you reach a high shelf without thinking about it?"). Passive — loaded press/pull logs.

entries.heading: E4 · Hip rehab
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild hip strength and function after labrum repair, FAI, gluteal tendinopathy, or chronic hip pain — once cleared.
**Technical signature**: `hip rehab post-clearance · maintenance kcal · glute strengthening + ROM + load tolerance · 12–24 weeks · medical-aware · primary-only initially`
⚠ **Post-clearance only.** Acute hip pain, post-surgical early phases, and undiagnosed hip pathology belong in clinical care.
**Who picks this**: Someone post-clearance with hip labrum repair (per surgeon timeline), femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome managed conservatively or post-arthroscopic, gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome), post-clearance from chronic hip pain.
**Physiological definition**: Hip rehab demands progressive load tolerance through the hip's full range, glute strengthening (the glute medius and minimus particularly underdeveloped in chronic hip presentations), pain-free ROM at end ranges, and gradual return to compound and impact loading. The LEAP trial (Mellor et al, 2018) demonstrated education + load-management exercise outperformed corticosteroid injection or wait-and-see for gluteal tendinopathy at 12 months.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight
Standard hydration and sleep
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (capacity + control, weeks 1–6 post-clearance)*: Glute bridges, side-lying abduction, clamshells, monster walks, isometric holds at end range. High frequency, low intensity. Hip mobility (90/90, hip flexor work).
*Phase 2 (loaded patterns, weeks 6–12)*: Hip thrust, single-leg RDL, Bulgarian split squat, step-ups. Progressive load with focus on form quality. Avoid end-range positions early in this phase if irritable.
*Phase 3 (strength rebuild, weeks 12+)*: Conventional squat and deadlift, single-leg power work, plyometric reintroduction. Sport-specific re-entry.
Conditioning: cycling and swimming unrestricted; running reintroduced gradually after Phase 3 capacity established.
**Typical duration**: 12–24 weeks. Gluteal tendinopathy specifically often takes 12+ months for full resolution per LEAP trial data.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3× lower-body strength sessions/week + daily mobility + 2–3× low-impact conditioning.
**Progress markers**:
Pain at loading stable or dropping (3/10 ceiling)
Single-leg strength approaching symmetry (>90% of uninjured side)
Hip ROM: pain-free flexion, abduction, rotation in their normal ranges
Loaded patterns: hip thrust to bodyweight × 1.5+, Bulgarian split squat with moderate load
Functional progress: stairs, then jogging, then return-to-activity without pain spike
Sleep on the affected side pain-free (gluteal tendinopathy night-pain marker)
**Common pitfalls**:
Skipping glute medius/minimus work: chronic hip presentations almost always involve these
Returning to running before adequate hip strength: re-aggravation cluster
Static stretching at painful end ranges: often aggravates tendinopathy
Treating it as a "tight hip" problem: chronic restriction is rarely just tightness — it's load tolerance
Discontinuing rehab when pain decreases: tissue capacity lags symptom resolution
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General health maintenance · Cardiovascular health focus (low-impact)
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Body recomposition · Build muscle / lean bulk
**Sources**:
Mellor, R. et al. (2018). Education plus exercise versus corticosteroid injection use versus a wait and see approach on global outcome and pain from gluteal tendinopathy. BMJ — LEAP trial.
Reiman, M., Matheson, J. (2013). Restricted hip mobility: clinical suggestions for self-mobilization and muscle re-education. Int J Sports Phys Ther.
Casartelli, N. et al. (2015). Hip muscle strength recovery after hip arthroscopy in a series of patients with symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement. Hip Int.
Griffin, D. et al. (2016). The Warwick Agreement on femoroacetabular impingement syndrome: an international consensus statement. Br J Sports Med.
Ganderton, C. et al. (2018). Gluteal Loading Versus Sham Exercises to Improve Pain and Dysfunction in Postmenopausal Women with Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome. J Womens Health.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Pain-free in sitting, walking, single-leg patterns. Symmetric strength and ROM (single-leg bridge endurance, hip abduction strength, Thomas test passing). Loaded hinge and single-leg squat tolerated.
*Window*: 4+ weeks pain-free under loaded patterns.
*Next step*: Graduated return to full strength training, with hip-specific accessory continued as maintenance.
*Detection*: Prompted weekly — pain + function. Prompted at milestones — single-leg balance/strength self-test guidance.

entries.heading: E5 · Achilles / calf rehab
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild Achilles and calf capacity after tendinopathy, post-strain, or post-rupture rehabilitation — once cleared.
**Technical signature**: `Achilles/calf rehab post-clearance · maintenance kcal · eccentric loading + heavy slow resistance + progressive impact · 12–24 weeks · medical-aware · primary-only initially`
⚠ **Post-clearance only.** Acute Achilles rupture or partial tear requires immediate clinical management.
**Who picks this**: Someone post-clearance with chronic mid-portion or insertional Achilles tendinopathy, post-Achilles-rupture rehabilitation (typically 4+ months post-injury), post-calf-strain return, or chronic calf-tightness/weakness limiting activity.
**Physiological definition**: Achilles tendinopathy responds to mechanical loading: classic Alfredson eccentric protocol (3×15 reps, 2× daily, 12 weeks) and the more recent heavy slow resistance approach (Beyer 2015) both demonstrate strong outcomes. The key principle: tendons need progressive load to remodel; rest-and-stretch underdoses the stimulus. Insertional tendinopathy may not tolerate full dorsiflexion-loaded eccentrics — modify with floor (no drop) variation.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance (deficits impair tendon remodeling)
Protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight
Vitamin C and gelatin/collagen 15g, 30–60 min pre-loading session, may support tendon adaptation
Sleep critical for tendon remodeling
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (eccentric or HSR base, weeks 1–6 post-clearance)*: Either Alfredson protocol (3×15 eccentric calf raises, straight and bent knee, 2×/day) or HSR (3×8–15 with 6-second tempo, 3×/week, progressively loaded). HSR has better adherence for many users and equivalent outcomes.
*Phase 2 (loaded calf + general lower body, weeks 6–12)*: Continue calf protocol, add bilateral squat, hip-dominant work (RDL), single-leg balance. Walking volume increases; running reintroduced cautiously.
*Phase 3 (impact return, weeks 12+)*: Progressive jumping (low to higher amplitude), running reintroduction (walk-run progression), sport-specific return.
Conditioning: cycling and swimming unrestricted throughout. Running reintroduced in Phase 2–3.
**Typical duration**: 12–24 weeks for tendinopathy. Post-rupture rehab is typically 6–12 months total.
**Frequency recommendation**: Calf protocol daily during Phase 1 (or 3×/week for HSR) + 3 strength sessions/week + low-impact cardio. Mobility daily for ankle and calf.
**Progress markers**:
Pain during loading stable or dropping (Silfverskiöld assessment, VISA-A score where applicable)
Single-leg calf raise capacity rising (rep count and weight)
Heel raise endurance: holding 25+ reps single-leg unloaded by Phase 2 end
Walking pain-free at full pace
Running reintroduction tolerated without pain spike
Sleep and morning stiffness improving
**Common pitfalls**:
Pure rest with stretching: under-doses the loading stimulus tendons need
Insertional tendinopathy with full-drop eccentrics: aggravation cycle (use floor variant instead)
Returning to running too aggressively: load progression too steep is leading re-aggravation cause
Discontinuing protocol once pain decreases: tendon capacity lags symptom relief
Skipping calf strengthening during running blocks long-term: original cause often resurfaces
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General strength (upper body unaffected) · Cardiovascular health focus (low-impact modalities)
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Alfredson, H. et al. (1998). Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis. Am J Sports Med.
Beyer, R. et al. (2015). Heavy Slow Resistance Versus Eccentric Training as Treatment for Achilles Tendinopathy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Am J Sports Med.
Silbernagel, K. et al. (2007). Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy. Am J Sports Med.
Mc Auliffe, S. et al. (2017). Can Ultrasound Imaging Predict the Development of Achilles and Patellar Tendinopathy? Br J Sports Med.
Cook, J., Purdam, C. (2009). Is tendon pathology a continuum? Br J Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Single-leg heel raise capacity restored (25+ reps full ROM each side, symmetric within 10%). Pain-free running progression if applicable (walk-run protocol completed). Hop test symmetric if higher-load goal.
*Window*: 4+ weeks pain-free under loaded running or hopping.
*Next step*: Return to full running volume OR sport-specific demands, with eccentric maintenance work continued.
*Detection*: Prompted weekly — morning stiffness rating, pain during loading. Prompted at milestone — guided heel raise count test.

entries.heading: E6 · Wrist / elbow rehab
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild grip and forearm capacity after tennis/golfer's elbow, climber's elbow, or wrist tendinopathy — once cleared.
**Technical signature**: `wrist/elbow rehab post-clearance · maintenance kcal · eccentric forearm + grip + load tolerance · 8–16 weeks · medical-aware · primary-only initially`
⚠ **Post-clearance only.** Acute or undiagnosed wrist/elbow pain requires clinical evaluation.
**Who picks this**: Someone post-clearance with lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow), medial epicondylalgia (golfer's elbow / climber's elbow), distal forearm tendinopathy, post-clearance from chronic wrist pain. Climbers and racquet-sport athletes are heavily represented; office workers also common.
**Physiological definition**: Lateral and medial epicondylalgia respond to progressive eccentric loading and isometrics — the classic Tyler protocol (Manias et al) and isometric pain-modulation approaches. As with Achilles, the principle is that tendons need progressive mechanical load to remodel, not rest-and-stretch. Heavy slow resistance also applicable. Grip strength is the integrated function output and should be tracked.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight
Vitamin C and gelatin pre-loading may support tendon adaptation (modest evidence)
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (isometric + eccentric base, weeks 1–4 post-clearance)*: Heavy isometrics (45-second holds at 70% effort, 5×) for pain modulation. Eccentric wrist extensions (lateral) or wrist flexions (medial) — Tyler twist or dumbbell variants, 3×15, daily.
*Phase 2 (loaded forearm + grip, weeks 4–10)*: Wrist curls and reverse curls progressing in load. Grip work (farmer's carries, hangboard for climbers when cleared, pinch holds). Reintroduce activity-specific patterns at sub-maximal load.
*Phase 3 (full loading + return, weeks 10+)*: Heavy grip work, full activity return (climbing, racquet sport, lifting) at progressive volume.
Lower-body and trunk training continues unaffected throughout.
**Typical duration**: 8–16 weeks. Chronic cases often require 6–12 months for full resolution.
**Frequency recommendation**: Forearm protocol daily during Phase 1 + 3× general strength sessions/week (with appropriate accommodations) + activity reintroduction per phase.
**Progress markers**:
Pain at loading stable or dropping (VAS or PRTEE — Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation)
Grip strength rising on dynamometer or rep tests
Pain-free wrist extension/flexion strength rising
Activity tolerance: longer climbing, racquet sport, or lifting sessions without pain spike
Sleep without pain on affected side
**Common pitfalls**:
Pure rest: under-doses load, doesn't drive remodeling
Returning to full activity once pain decreases: tendon capacity lags symptom relief
Cortisone-as-primary-treatment: short-term relief, often poorer long-term outcomes than progressive loading
Climbers continuing hangboard during acute phase: aggravation cycle
Ignoring upstream contributors: shoulder weakness, mobility, technique often relevant
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General strength (lower body and trunk unaffected) · Cardiovascular health focus
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Climbing / bouldering (until cleared) · Racquet sports (until cleared) · Build muscle / lean bulk
**Sources**:
Tyler, T. et al. (2010). Adding isolated wrist extensor eccentric exercise to standard treatment for chronic lateral epicondylosis: a prospective randomized trial. J Shoulder Elbow Surg.
Manias, P., Stasinopoulos, D. (2006). A controlled clinical pilot trial to study the effectiveness of ice as a supplement to the exercise programme for the management of lateral elbow tendinopathy. Br J Sports Med.
Coombes, B. et al. (2013). Effect of corticosteroid injection, physiotherapy, or both on clinical outcomes in patients with unilateral lateral epicondylalgia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA.
Bisset, L. et al. (2005). A systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials on physical interventions for lateral epicondylalgia. Br J Sports Med.
Schöffl, V. et al. (2018). The epidemiology of injury in mountaineering, rock and ice climbing. Med Sport Sci.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Pain-free during gripping, loaded carry, pressing/pulling. Eccentric loading protocol completed (e.g., Tyler twist for lateral epicondylitis). Symmetric grip strength. Sport-specific demand tolerated (climbing crimps, racquet swings, lifting at full load).
*Window*: 4+ weeks pain-free under target load.
*Next step*: Return to full training with maintenance eccentric/strengthening continued.
*Detection*: Prompted weekly — pain during specific tasks. Passive — grip strength log if measured, load progression on related lifts.

entries.heading: E7 · Return-to-training after extended pause
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild capacity after a long pause — post-surgery (cleared), post-illness, or 3+ months away from training.
**Technical signature**: `return-to-training · maintenance kcal · graded reentry · 8–16 weeks · primary-only`
**Who picks this**: Someone returning after post-surgical clearance (general, not surgery-specific — those use E1–E6), post-illness recovery (cleared by physician for return), 3+ months away from structured training (relocation, life event, injury that has now resolved), or post-extended-rest period for any reason. Distinct from rehab goals (which target a specific tissue) — this targets general capacity-rebuilding.
**Physiological definition**: Detraining produces measurable losses across all systems: strength (~10% in 4 weeks of zero training, accelerating thereafter), aerobic capacity (~10% in 3 weeks, larger in less-trained individuals), tendon and connective tissue capacity (slowest to detrain but slowest to rebuild), neural drive and movement quality. The rebuild is faster than the original build (muscle memory effects) but isn't instantaneous and rushing it produces injury cluster. Graded reentry across 8–16 weeks restores baseline before advancing to a directional goal.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg body weight
Sleep prioritized (rebuilding under-recovered tissue is particularly sleep-dependent)
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (volume reentry, weeks 1–4)*: Submaximal full-body strength (compound machines, bodyweight, light free weight), Zone 2 walking/cycling. Sets at RPE 5–7. The goal is reintroducing movement patterns and rebuilding tissue tolerance, not progress.
*Phase 2 (load + complexity, weeks 4–10)*: Progressive load increase, free-weight reintroduction, full ROM work, light conditioning intervals. Approach (but stay below) pre-pause working loads.
*Phase 3 (capacity rebuild, weeks 10+)*: Full training stimulus, approaching pre-pause baseline. Transition to a directional goal once baseline restored.
Conditioning matched to phase: easy cardio in Phase 1, progressive in Phase 2, full structure in Phase 3.
**Typical duration**: 8–16 weeks. Length depends on pause duration: 3-month pause might need 8 weeks; 12+ month pause needs 16+ weeks.
**Frequency recommendation**:
Phase 1: 3× full-body sessions + 2–3× walking
Phase 2: 3–4× strength + 2× conditioning
Phase 3: full programming per chosen subsequent goal
**Progress markers**:
Pre-pause strength baseline approached and re-passed
Pre-pause conditioning baseline approached
Movement quality restored on key compound patterns
No injury during reentry (most concrete marker of well-paced rebuild)
Recovery (sleep, HRV) stable across phases
Confidence and consistency: subjective marker, often the rate-limiting psychological factor for long pauses
**Common pitfalls**:
Trying to "pick up where you left off": injury cluster in week 1–4
Using motivation peaks to push too hard early: pause-rebuild-pause cycle
Skipping the reentry phase entirely: most common cause of post-pause injury
Treating it as a punishment for the pause: counterproductive psychology, often drives repeat pause
Comparing current numbers to pre-pause numbers: useful as direction, demotivating as standard
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General health maintenance · Cardiovascular health focus · Sustainable fat loss only if pause was associated with weight gain and capacity allows
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Build muscle / lean bulk during early reentry · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Mujika, I., Padilla, S. (2000). Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med.
Mujika, I., Padilla, S. (2000). Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part II: Long term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med.
Bosquet, L. et al. (2013). Effect of training cessation on muscular performance: a meta-analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports.
Suchomel, T. et al. (2018). The importance of muscular strength: training considerations. Sports Med.
Gabbett, T. (2016). The training-injury prevention paradox. Br J Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: 4 consecutive weeks of full programmed sessions completed without injury or excessive soreness. Capacity rebuilt to ~70-80% of pre-pause level (or established new baseline). User reports training "feels normal" again.
*Window*: 4-week consistency window AND capacity benchmark reached.
*Next step*: Transition to user's chosen directional goal (most common: A2, A4, B1, or D1).
*Detection*: Passive — session completion rate, strength progression. Prompted at week 4: "Does training feel like a routine again, or still a project?"

entries.heading: F1 · Pregnancy — early (T1)
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train through your first trimester — adapt for fatigue, maintain capacity, no new max efforts.
**Technical signature**: `pregnancy T1 · maintenance to slight surplus · maintain capacity, fatigue-aware · 12 weeks · medical-aware · primary-only`
⚠ **Confirm with your prenatal care provider that exercise is appropriate for your specific pregnancy.** Conditions like placenta previa, preeclampsia, severe anemia, or restricted cervix change the picture significantly. The KB is a training-design tool that runs alongside prenatal care, not in place of it.
**Who picks this**: Someone in the first trimester (weeks 1–13) of an uncomplicated pregnancy who wants to keep training. Includes both established trainers continuing existing routines and recently active people maintaining baseline activity. Not for users with high-risk pregnancies, contraindications listed by ACOG, or those advised against exercise by their care provider.
**Physiological definition**: First trimester brings hormonal shifts (rising progesterone and hCG drive fatigue, nausea, sleep disruption), no significant biomechanical changes yet, and no fetal heat-stress concerns at typical training intensities. ACOG (2020) supports continued exercise for healthy pregnant individuals at intensities and modalities they were performing pre-pregnancy. New maximum efforts and significant load progression are deferred — the goal is maintaining capacity, not building peak. Caloric needs increase only modestly in T1 (~0–150 kcal/day depending on activity).
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance to slight surplus (~+0–150 kcal in T1)
Protein 1.6–1.8 g/kg pre-pregnancy body weight
Folate per prenatal vitamin
Iron monitored per provider (anemia is common and affects capacity)
Hydration increased baseline; avoid significant dehydration
Listen to nausea — eating smaller, more frequent meals usually helps
**Dominant training type**: Maintain pre-pregnancy training pattern at moderate-to-submaximal intensity. Strength: continue compound and accessory work at RPE 6–8, no new 1RM attempts. Conditioning: continue at moderate intensity (HR-based zones unreliable in pregnancy due to elevated baseline; use RPE — "talk test"). Avoid hot environments, high-altitude exertion, contact sports, prolonged supine work. Mobility: maintain; avoid extreme range as ligament laxity rises (relaxin).
**Typical duration**: 12 weeks (or until transitioning to F2). Volume often reduces naturally due to fatigue/nausea — that's appropriate.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3–5 sessions/week, scaled to energy and well-being on the day. Skip sessions when severely fatigued or nauseated; that's information, not failure.
**Progress markers**:
Maintenance of pre-pregnancy strength and conditioning
No symptoms suggesting need for medical attention (vaginal bleeding, severe shortness of breath at low intensity, chest pain, regular contractions, fluid leakage, severe headache)
Energy and recovery variable in T1, expect ups and downs
Adherence to ACOG warning signs — any of these: stop, contact provider
**Common pitfalls**:
"Eating for two" early: T1 caloric increase is minimal
Pushing through severe fatigue or nausea: T1 fatigue is hormonal, not improved by training
Continuing max effort lifting: defer 1RM attempts and high-RPE max work
Failing to communicate with care provider: any new symptoms warrant a check-in
Starting a brand-new training modality in T1: T1 is for maintenance, not new capacity
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General health maintenance · Cardiovascular health focus
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Build muscle / lean bulk · Body recomposition · Sustainable fat loss / Major weight loss
**Sources**:
ACOG (2020, reaffirmed 2023). Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period. Committee Opinion 804. Obstet Gynecol.
Mottola, M. et al. (2018). 2019 Canadian guideline for physical activity throughout pregnancy. Br J Sports Med.
Davenport, M. et al. (2019). Prenatal exercise for the prevention of gestational diabetes mellitus and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med.
Bø, K. et al. (2016). Exercise and pregnancy in recreational and elite athletes: 2016/2017 evidence summary. Br J Sports Med.
IOC consensus (2017). Exercise and pregnancy in recreational and elite athletes: 2016 evidence summary from the IOC expert group meeting. Br J Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Reached end of trimester 1 (~week 12-14) with consistent appropriate training, no medical contraindications arising, baseline conditioning maintained. Note: this goal is phase-based, not performance-based.
*Window*: Phase transition = T1 end. Marker is "made it through with consistent training."
*Next step*: Transition to F2 (Pregnancy — mid) automatically at gestational marker.
*Detection*: Prompted — gestational week tracking, monthly check-ins on training tolerance and any medical guidance changes.

entries.heading: F2 · Pregnancy — mid (T2 + early T3)
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train through second trimester and early third — continue with positional adjustments and pelvic floor priority.
**Technical signature**: `pregnancy T2 + early T3 · slight surplus (+200–300 kcal) · positional + pelvic floor focus · ~16 weeks · medical-aware · primary-only`
⚠ **Continue prenatal care; ensure care provider supports continued training. Symptoms requiring immediate cessation and medical contact: vaginal bleeding, regular painful contractions, fluid leakage, severe shortness of breath at rest, persistent chest pain, severe headache, calf pain or swelling (DVT signs), decreased fetal movement (after quickening typically week 18–22).**
**Who picks this**: Someone in second trimester (weeks 14–27) and early third trimester (weeks 28–32) of uncomplicated pregnancy who wants to continue training. Often the most physically capable phase of pregnancy.
**Physiological definition**: Mid-pregnancy brings progressive belly growth, shifting center of gravity (anterior pelvic tilt rises), increasing ligament laxity (relaxin peaks late T2), expanding blood volume (~30–50% increase by T3), elevated resting HR, and expanding ribcage. Supine training becomes less appropriate after ~16 weeks (vena cava compression). Pelvic floor work becomes priority for delivery preparation and postpartum trajectory.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy surplus +200–300 kcal/day in T2, +400+ in late T2/early T3
Protein 1.6–1.8 g/kg pre-pregnancy weight
Iron continue monitoring with provider
Hydration significantly elevated needs given blood volume expansion
Avoid prolonged fasting (impacts fetal glucose supply)
**Dominant training type**: Strength: continue compounds with positional modifications (incline bench replaces flat after ~20 weeks; offset/staggered stance for hinging; avoid heavy front-loaded squats as belly grows). Pelvic floor: explicit work introduced — connection-and-release patterns rather than pure Kegels-to-failure. Conditioning: continue at moderate intensity, modality-flexible (cycling, swimming, walking, low-impact stair work). Mobility: hip work prioritized for delivery prep; avoid extreme passive ranges given laxity. Diastasis recti awareness: avoid exercises that produce visible doming.
**Typical duration**: ~16 weeks (T2 + early T3). Transition to F3 around week 28–32.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3–5 sessions/week. Energy is often best in T2.
**Progress markers**:
Continued capacity: strength maintained, conditioning adequate
No ACOG warning signs
Pelvic floor connection: ability to consciously contract and release
No diastasis worsening (visible inter-rectus distance growing significantly)
Recovery and sleep manageable
Birth preparation goals: hip mobility maintained, breath-and-pelvic-floor coordination
**Common pitfalls**:
Continuing prone or fully supine work after ~16 weeks
Aggressive crunching or planks producing doming: contributes to diastasis recti
Skipping pelvic floor work: postpartum recovery harder without baseline awareness
"Keep doing what you did pre-pregnancy" past the point modifications are needed
Ignoring back/SI joint pain as ligament laxity rises
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health (especially hip) · General health maintenance · Cardiovascular health focus
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Build muscle / lean bulk · Sustainable fat loss / Major weight loss · Body recomposition
**Sources**:
ACOG Committee Opinion 804 (2020/2023). Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy.
Mottola, M. et al. (2018). 2019 Canadian guideline for physical activity throughout pregnancy. Br J Sports Med.
Sperstad, J. et al. (2016). Diastasis recti abdominis during pregnancy and 12 months after childbirth: prevalence, risk factors and report of lumbopelvic pain. Br J Sports Med.
Bø, K. et al. (2017). Exercise and pregnancy in recreational and elite athletes: 2016/2017 evidence summary, part 5. Br J Sports Med.
Davenport, M. et al. (2018). Prenatal exercise (including pelvic floor muscle training) and urinary incontinence during and following pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Reached end of T2 / start of T3 (~week 28) with maintained training adapted to changing body. No red-flag symptoms during loading. Strength preserved at adapted loads.
*Window*: Phase transition = end of T2.
*Next step*: Transition to F3 (Pregnancy — late) automatically at gestational marker.
*Detection*: Prompted — gestational tracking, weekly check-in on symptom watch list.

entries.heading: F3 · Pregnancy — late (late T3)
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train through the final stretch — delivery preparation, mobility, low-intensity load.
**Technical signature**: `pregnancy late T3 · surplus +400+ kcal · delivery prep + mobility + low-intensity · ~6–10 weeks · medical-aware · primary-only`
⚠ **Continue prenatal care. Same warning signs from T1/T2 apply. The closer to term, the more session-by-session adaptation matters.**
**Who picks this**: Someone in late third trimester (weeks 32+) of uncomplicated pregnancy who wants to remain active. Training shifts substantially — capacity-building is gone, delivery prep takes over.
**Physiological definition**: Late pregnancy brings significant biomechanical change: maximal belly volume, peak ligament laxity, larger center-of-gravity shift, often pelvic discomfort or pubic symphysis pain, reduced cardiopulmonary reserve. Goal shifts from training adaptation to: maintaining circulation, supporting delivery preparation through mobility and pelvic floor work, managing weight gain trajectory, and supporting mental wellbeing.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy surplus +400+ kcal/day depending on activity and individual
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg pre-pregnancy weight
Hydration continues elevated; pay attention to swelling patterns
Iron continued provider monitoring
**Dominant training type**: Walking primary modality — daily walking matters for circulation and mood. Strength: low-load full-body 1–2× weekly using machines, dumbbells, bodyweight. Form quality > load. Pelvic floor: continued connection-and-release, breath coordination, pre-delivery breath patterns. Mobility: hip openers, deep squat practice, cat-cow, child's pose adaptations — preparation for delivery positions. Conditioning: walking, swimming if accessible, stationary cycling.
**Typical duration**: ~6–10 weeks (weeks 32 to delivery). Transitions immediately into F4 post-delivery.
**Frequency recommendation**: Daily walking + 2–3× modified strength + 1–2× dedicated mobility/pelvic floor sessions. Adjust to comfort.
**Progress markers**:
Continued daily activity (walking minutes maintained)
Pelvic floor connection deepening
Hip mobility for delivery positions (deep squat, kneeling, side-lying)
No ACOG warning signs
Sleep manageable given physical limitations
Subjective: feeling capable and prepared rather than exhausted
**Common pitfalls**:
Trying to "stay in shape" with high-intensity work: not the season for it
Stopping all activity from week 32: walking and mobility serve circulation, mood, and delivery prep
Skipping pelvic floor work because "delivery is delivery": pre-delivery practice translates to faster postpartum recovery
Ignoring pubic symphysis or pelvic girdle pain: modify, narrow stance, avoid asymmetric loading
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health (delivery preparation) · General health maintenance
**Incompatible goals**: Everything performance-oriented (Strength peak, race prep, hypertrophy, etc.)
**Sources**:
ACOG Committee Opinion 804 (2020/2023).
Mottola, M. et al. (2018). 2019 Canadian guideline for physical activity throughout pregnancy. Br J Sports Med.
Sapsford, R. et al. (2010). Sitting posture affects pelvic floor muscle activity in parous women. Aust J Physiother.
Davenport, M. et al. (2018). Prenatal exercise and incidence of postpartum depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med.
Hartmann, K., Viswanathan, M. et al. (2005). Outcomes of routine episiotomy: a systematic review. JAMA.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Reached delivery with maintained appropriate activity (typically walking, light loaded work, mobility, prep exercises). Pelvic floor prepared. Birth plan supportive activities completed if user-set.
*Window*: Phase = delivery.
*Next step*: Transition to F4 (Postpartum reconditioning) after postnatal medical clearance (typically 6-week check-up, longer for c-section).
*Detection*: Prompted — gestational tracking. Post-delivery confirmation: "Delivered? Any clearance from your provider for activity?" routes to F4 entry phase.

entries.heading: F4 · Postpartum reconditioning
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Rebuild after birth — pelvic floor and core restoration first, then progressive return to strength.
**Technical signature**: `postpartum reconditioning · maintenance to slight surplus (lactation +330–500 kcal) · pelvic floor + core + graded reentry · 12–24+ weeks · medical-aware · primary-only`
⚠ **Begin only after postnatal clearance — typically the 6-week check-up for uncomplicated vaginal birth, longer for cesarean section or complications. Pelvic floor symptoms (incontinence, prolapse sensation, pain), diastasis recti beyond ~2 finger-widths, or any concerning postpartum signs warrant evaluation by a pelvic floor physiotherapist before starting structured strength work.**
**Who picks this**: Someone post-cleared after childbirth wanting structured reconditioning. Typical entry is 6–12 weeks postpartum after vaginal birth, longer for c-section. Lactation continues to affect energy needs and joint laxity for many users.
**Physiological definition**: Postpartum brings gradual hormonal normalization, pelvic floor and core healing, persistent ligament laxity (continues for ~3–6 months postpartum, longer if breastfeeding), potential diastasis recti, often poor sleep and unpredictable schedules, and an athlete returning from significant detraining. The progression must respect the pelvic floor — symptoms during loading (leaking, heaviness, pain) signal premature progression.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance (non-lactating) or +330–500 kcal (lactating)
Protein 1.8–2.0 g/kg body weight
Hydration significantly elevated if breastfeeding
Avoid aggressive deficits while lactating (impacts milk supply and postpartum recovery)
**Dominant training type**: Phased.
*Phase 1 (foundation, weeks 6–12 postpartum or post-clearance)*: Pelvic floor reconnection (release as well as activation), diaphragmatic breathing, deep core (transverse abdominis), glute bridges, walking. No high-impact, no heavy lifting, no plank holds in early phase. Sessions short (20–30 min).
*Phase 2 (loaded patterns, weeks 12–20)*: Goblet squat, hip thrust, deadlift with kettlebell, push-pull at moderate load. Progressively introduce stand-up movements. Continue pelvic floor and core work daily.
*Phase 3 (capacity rebuild, weeks 20+)*: Progress to compound lifts at moderate-to-heavy load. Reintroduce running if previously a runner, in walk-run progression and only with no pelvic floor symptoms. Plyometric reintroduction last.
Conditioning: walking from week 1 post-clearance. Swimming and cycling once cleared. Running only when capacity supports it — often 4–6 months postpartum or later.
**Typical duration**: 12–24+ weeks for full reconditioning. Variable per individual.
**Frequency recommendation**:
Phase 1: 2–3× short sessions/week + daily walking
Phase 2: 3× strength + walking
Phase 3: full programming per chosen subsequent goal
**Progress markers**:
Pelvic floor symptoms absent or substantially reduced
Diastasis recti gap closing or stable; no doming on exertion
Strength rebuilding: load progressing on key compounds
Cesarean scar pain-free at full ROM (typically by week 12)
Sleep and recovery adapting to family rhythm
Subjective: feeling like an athlete again, gradually
**Common pitfalls**:
Returning to running before pelvic floor capacity supports it
Skipping pelvic floor PT when symptoms are present
Aggressive ab work in early postpartum: doming, persistent diastasis
Aggressive caloric deficit while breastfeeding
"Snap back" pressure narrative: irrelevant to durable rebuild
Skipping the foundation phase: short-term perceived progress, long-term injury cluster
**Compatible secondary goals**: Mobility & joint health · General health maintenance · Cardiovascular health focus · Sustainable fat loss only after full reconditioning + (if breastfeeding) milk supply unaffected
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak · Race prep (any distance) · Build muscle / lean bulk during reconditioning · Body recomposition during early phases · Major weight loss during lactation
**Sources**:
ACOG Committee Opinion 804 (2020/2023). Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period.
Mottola, M. et al. (2018). 2019 Canadian guideline for physical activity throughout pregnancy. Br J Sports Med.
Goom, T., Donnelly, G., Brockwell, E. (2019). Returning to running postnatal — guidelines for medical, health and fitness professionals managing this population. Open access white paper, BJSM endorsed.
Sperstad, J. et al. (2016). Diastasis recti abdominis during pregnancy and 12 months after childbirth. Br J Sports Med.
Bø, K. et al. (2017). Exercise and pregnancy in recreational and elite athletes: 2016/2017 evidence summary. Br J Sports Med.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: All three phases completed: Phase 1 (foundation, pelvic floor + deep core reconnection, no symptoms during daily activity), Phase 2 (loaded patterns tolerated, no doming or pelvic floor symptoms under load), Phase 3 (full compound lifts at moderate-heavy load, plyometric reintroduction tolerated if applicable). Pelvic floor symptoms absent for 4+ weeks. Diastasis closed or stable with no doming.
*Window*: Variable per individual (12-24+ weeks total). Each phase = its own milestone with 4-week stable window before progression.
*Next step*: Transition to user's chosen post-postpartum goal (commonly A2, A4, B1, D1) with postpartum-aware programming maintained where relevant.
*Detection*: Prompted weekly during Phases 1-2 — pelvic floor symptom check, doming check, sleep/energy. Prompted at phase transitions — guided self-assessment. Passive — load progression in Phase 3.

entries.heading: F5 · Menopause / perimenopause-aware training
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train through perimenopause and menopause — heavy compound work, recovery emphasis, and bone density priority.
**Technical signature**: `peri/post-menopausal training · maintenance kcal · heavy strength + impact + recovery emphasis · open-ended · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Women in perimenopause (often 40s, sometimes earlier) or post-menopause (typically 50s+) wanting training adapted to the hormonal context. Common motivators: bone density concerns, body composition shifts, sleep changes, energy fluctuations, vasomotor symptoms.
**Physiological definition**: Estrogen decline drives meaningful physiological changes: accelerated bone density loss (especially in the 5–7 years around menopause), shift in body composition (visceral fat tendency rising, muscle mass dropping faster without intervention), changes in sleep architecture and thermoregulation, reduced exercise-induced muscle protein synthesis response, and longer recovery between hard sessions. Heavy resistance training and impact work directly counter the bone density loss and provide the strongest body composition lever.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance (chronic deficits worsen vasomotor symptoms and bone loss)
Protein 2.0–2.4 g/kg body weight
Adequate calcium and vitamin D
Sleep is non-negotiable for body composition and mood stability
Caffeine and alcohol moderation supports sleep quality
**Dominant training type**: Strength: heavy compound work prioritized (squat, deadlift, hip thrust, overhead press, bench, row at 80–85% 1RM, 3–5 sets of 3–6 reps). LIFTMOR-style protocols evidence-based for bone density. Impact: 2–3× weekly weighted jumping, hopping, or impact-loading patterns. Conditioning: 2–3× Zone 2/week + 1× HIIT (HIIT helpful for body composition in this population specifically) — kept well-spaced from heavy strength. Mobility: daily; especially shoulder and hip. Recovery: actively managed (sleep schedule, sauna/cold, low-stress active recovery).
**Typical duration**: Open-ended.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3 heavy strength + 1× HIIT + 2× Zone 2 + daily mobility + impact work distributed across the week.
**Progress markers**:
Strength: 1–5RM rising on heavy compounds
DEXA bone density (clinical) stable or improving over 12-month windows
Body composition stable or improving (waist, lean mass)
Sleep stable, ≥7 hours
Vasomotor symptoms variable; training usually stabilizes them long-term
Mood and energy stable across the cycle (perimenopause) or steady (post)
**Common pitfalls**:
Light-load training only: misses the bone density and muscle preservation drivers
Adding lots of long-duration cardio: contributes to muscle loss
Inadequate protein: impacts both muscle preservation and recovery
Underestimating recovery needs: sessions that worked at 30 may need more recovery at 50
Aggressive caloric deficit: backfires for body composition, sleep, and bone health
**Compatible secondary goals**: Bone density (high overlap) · General strength · Mobility & joint health · Cardiovascular health focus · General health maintenance · Metabolic health
**Incompatible goals**: Race prep (any distance) unless longstanding pursuit and adapted accordingly · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Watson, S. et al. (2018). High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial. J Bone Miner Res.
Sims, S. ROAR: How to Match Your Food and Fitness to Your Female Physiology (Rodale, 2016).
Hayes, L. et al. (2018). Resistance Training and Older Women: Considerations and Guidelines for Exercise Practitioners. Strength Cond J.
Davis, S. et al. (2015). Menopause. Nat Rev Dis Primers.
The Menopause Society (formerly NAMS) Position Statements on hormone therapy and management of menopausal symptoms.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: This is an open-ended goal — no graduation. Markers of "training is working for this phase of life": symptom impact on training reduced (hot flashes during sessions, sleep quality), strength maintained or improved across blocks, bone density stable or improving (if measured), mood/energy reported stable.
*Window*: Rolling quarterly review — there is no end-point.
*Next step*: Continue indefinitely. Periodic re-evaluation of programming per symptom changes. Compatible with most secondary goals.
*Detection*: Prompted quarterly — "How is training feeling this quarter? Symptoms affecting sessions?" Passive — strength logs, session completion.

entries.heading: F6 · Senior fitness (60+)
entries.content_markdown:
**Description** *(consumer)*: Train for capability, balance, and fall prevention — meaningful strength built deliberately at any age.
**Technical signature**: `senior fitness 60+ · maintenance kcal · strength + power + balance + Zone 2 · open-ended · primary or compatible-secondary`
**Who picks this**: Adults 60+ who want to maintain or build physical capability. Suitable for first-time trainers in this age group through advanced lifters who happen to be older. Also fits 50+ users prioritizing longevity-oriented training.
**Physiological definition**: Aging produces gradual sarcopenia (~3–8% muscle loss per decade after 30, accelerating after 60), faster decline in power than strength (Type II fiber loss), balance and proprioception decline, slower recovery, bone density decline, often reduced fasting protein synthesis response (compensable with higher protein intake). Resistance training gains in older adults are robust — 60- to 90-year-olds gain strength on similar trajectories as younger adults when training appropriately. Power training has stronger transfer to functional capacity than slow heavy lifting alone for this population.
**Calorie / nutrition strategy**:
Energy maintenance
Protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg body weight (higher end of range)
Vitamin D and calcium adequacy verified
Hydration prioritized (thirst signal blunts with age)
**Dominant training type**: Strength: compound lifts adapted to capability — squat (or sit-to-stand progression), deadlift (or hip hinge), pressing, rowing, carries. Sets of 6–12, RPE 6–8. Power: 1–2× weekly explosive work — fast concentric on lifts (light load moved fast), medicine ball throws, jumps if cleared. Balance: daily — single-leg stance, tandem walk, side stepping. 5–10 min total. Conditioning: Zone 2 (walking, cycling, swimming) 3–4× weekly. HIIT optional. Mobility: daily, especially hip and shoulder.
**Typical duration**: Open-ended.
**Frequency recommendation**: 3–4 strength sessions + daily walking + 2–3 dedicated balance/mobility windows + 1× power session.
**Progress markers**:
Strength rising on key compound patterns
Functional tests: 5× sit-to-stand time dropping, single-leg stance time rising, gait speed maintained or improving
Stair-climbing capacity stable or rising
Bone density (DEXA, 12-month intervals) stable or improving
Falls in past year: zero
Cognitive function: training shows protective effects in this domain
**Common pitfalls**:
Training "carefully" with light loads forever: misses the strength and power adaptation drivers
Skipping power work: power declines faster than strength and matters more for daily function
Avoiding ground-based work permanently: getting up from the floor is functional capacity
Inadequate protein: muscle loss accelerates without it
Frailty fatalism: "I'm too old for that" — research consistently disproves this
Skipping balance work: fall prevention is high-leverage
**Compatible secondary goals**: Bone density · General strength · Mobility & joint health · Cardiovascular health focus · General health maintenance · Metabolic health
**Incompatible goals**: Strength peak (relatively) · Race prep — long distance (relatively) · Body recomposition · Major weight loss
**Sources**:
Fragala, M. et al. (2019). Resistance Training for Older Adults: Position Statement From the National Strength and Conditioning Association. J Strength Cond Res.
Cadore, E. et al. (2014). Effects of different exercise interventions on risk of falls, gait ability, and balance in physically frail older adults: a systematic review. Rejuvenation Res.
Phillips, S. et al. (2016). Protein "requirements" beyond the RDA: implications for optimizing health. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab.
Liu, C., Latham, N. (2009). Progressive resistance strength training for improving physical function in older adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev.
Reid, K., Fielding, R. (2012). Skeletal muscle power: a critical determinant of physical functioning in older adults. Exerc Sport Sci Rev.
**Achievement markers**:
*Signal*: Open-ended goal. Markers: independence in daily activities preserved/improved, balance test maintained (single-leg stand, sit-to-stand count), strength preserved (key compounds at maintained or improved loads), absence of injury/fall events.
*Window*: Rolling quarterly review.
*Next step*: Continue indefinitely. Periodic re-evaluation per life-context changes.
*Detection*: Prompted quarterly — guided balance and functional self-tests, daily-activity confidence check. Passive — strength logs.
